entries.title: DMV High School Football Players of Week 2
entries.summary: This weekend’s standouts included a bruising back from Gonzaga and a ball hawk from C.G. Woodson.
entries.content:
With Maryland public schools kicking off this past weekend, high school football season is officially in full swing in the D.C. area. Here’s who made their mark in Week 2:

David Anderson, senior, quarterback, Theodore Roosevelt

With Anderson under center, the Roughriders’ offense exploded in a season-opening 40-15 victory over KIPP. The senior torched the Bulldogs, passing for 252 passing and three touchdowns. He also added a fourth score on the ground as Roosevelt kicked off a new year with a statement victory. Anderson’s connection with senior wide receiver Gabe Hudgens could make for one of the strongest combinations in the city as coach Chris Harden’s team looks to bounce back from last year’s dramatic playoff loss to Dunbar.

Sign up for the NOTUS Metro newsletter for essential coverage of the D.C. region.

Asheton Burton, senior, running back, Gonzaga

After a slew of early turnovers Thursday against Coolidge, Gonzaga’s offense needed a spark. With the game still scoreless midway through the second quarter, the Eagles handed the ball to Burton, the team’s bruising running back, nine straight times and the senior marched his team down the field. Burton scored from 2 yards out for the game’s first points, then pulled off a second-half hat trick with three more touchdown runs as Gonzaga rolled to a 33-0 victory. Burton’s final touchdown run of the night was arguably his most impressive as he bulldozed his way through a horde of Coolidge defenders for a 14-yard score.

Corey Smith Jr., junior, wide receiver, Good Counsel

The Falcons earned their first win of the Sal Gorgone era in thrilling fashion Friday, turning New Jersey powerhouse Bergen Catholic away at the goal line in the closing seconds of the game to seal a 41-39 win. Smith, a towering 6-foot-5, 210-pound receiver whose Division I offer list includes Maryland and Virginia Tech, caught three touchdowns and racked up 131 receiving yards. “What a beautiful athlete,” Gorgone said of Smith after the win. “He’s a playmaker, and he makes those plays in clutch moments.”

Darren Theobald, senior, defensive back, C.G. Woodson

Theobald pulled down three interceptions for the Cavaliers in Thursday’s 28-7 victory over Edison. The first came on the game’s opening drive, when the senior grabbed an Eagles pass in the corner of the end zone to squash Edison’s momentum. The second came with the game knotted at 7 in the third quarter, and it was followed by a long Woodson touchdown drive. Theobald’s busy night peaked in the fourth quarter when he hauled in a 33-yard receiving touchdown at wide receiver before switching to defense and snatching a third pick to clinch a victory. Theobald and the Cavaliers will look to replicate their defensive performance next week against Oakton, whose high-powered offense is averaging 49 points per game.

Jamie White Jr., senior, defensive back, Quince Orchard

It didn’t take long for White, a senior transfer from St. Frances, to make an impact with the Cougars. In his first game, the defensive back nabbed an interception on the first play from scrimmage. It would be his first of three on the night. The Cougars, two-time defending Maryland 4A champions, earned their 28th straight victory with a 28-0 win over Paint Branch. With White and three-star senior Rico Jackson patrolling the secondary and senior Pittsburgh commit Jaheim Bond wreaking havoc up front, coach John Kelley’s defense is again among the area’s best.

To nominate a local player for next week’s roundup, send us an email with their name and stats. See last week’s selections here.

entries.title: Self-Funders Are Still Terrible at Getting Themselves Elected
entries.summary: Ultrarich politicians — in most cases — can’t buy a seat in Congress.
entries.content:
It’s still exceedingly difficult to buy oneself a seat in Congress.

During the 2026 midterms, a record number of wealthy Americans — 69 — have spent more than $1 million of their own money to support their campaigns for federal office.

And with primary season ending in the next several days with contests in New Hampshire, Rhode Island and Delaware, about two-thirds of these self-funding candidates have turned out to be losers who couldn’t advance to the November general election.
https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/ub0ox/4/Those who bet big on themselves to win their races for Congress collectively loaned their campaigns $160 million.

At the extreme, former Rep. David Trone burned through about $25 million of his own cash only to lose in his Maryland 6th Congressional District primary by 7 percentage points to fellow Democratic Rep. April McClain Delaney.
David.Trone.1 (5515x3677, AR: 1.50)In Arizona, businessman Daniel Keenan spent $1.6 million on his failed bid to replace Republican Rep. Andy Biggs.

Keenan says the run was well worth it even if he lost the Republican primary to former county sheriff Mark Lamb in July.

“I did it to contribute to my country, to do the best I can to make my country better off for my kids,” he said. “It was never for personal gain or ego or anything like that.”

Keenan also expects to one day run again: “I worked my butt off … went from polling at 1% to capturing nearly 42% of the vote. I think we ran a really good campaign and set myself up well for future runs.”

Still, Keenan said he was surprised by “the amount of prominent Republicans who privately reached out to me and supported me” but wouldn’t do so publicly.

“I was the most Trump-aligned candidate and again defending all those policies at every chance I could, and it was difficult not getting the support from the White House,” he said.

On the other end of that spectrum is Thomas Chalifoux, a retired Army colonel and businessman who sought the Republican nomination in Florida’s 9th Congressional District.

Chalifoux placed third in the Republican primary, having spent upward of $2 million on his ultimately failed campaign. It was a worse showing than his 2024 bid for the same seat, which saw him secure the GOP nomination but lose in the general election to Democratic Rep. Darren Soto.

That race also cost him upward of $2 million — a fraction of his net worth, which sits at around $270 million, per his most recent federal financial disclosure. Still, he is quick to point out: “I started with nothing, just like Elon Musk.”

Chalifoux previously taught military strategy at the Army Command and General Staff College and, more than anything, seemed disappointed he would not have the chance to go against the “bunch of rubber stamps in Congress” who have supported President Donald Trump’s war with Iran.

“The Iran ‘Epic Fury’ is just poorly, poorly planned. We've got a mess on our hands, and it makes American military power look much worse,” Chalifoux said. Trump “created a climate where no one wants to disagree because he's very vindictive.”Might he try a third time come 2028?

“I don't know. I'm 78 … people look at that as being too old. I'm not too old,” he said, noting he is a “world-class bodybuilder” whose mother “is over 100, so I've got that longevity in my family.”

Earlier this year, Keith Gross and John Fleming, candidates for Florida’s 2nd Congressional District and U.S. Senate in Louisiana, respectively, each spent around $12 million on their failed primary campaigns.
John.Fleming (7023x4682, AR: 1.50)Democrat Peter Chatzky entered, then exited, the race for New York's 17th Congressional District after the resurfacing of lewd social media posts in March. He ultimately recouped $10.7 million of the $11.3 million he had loaned his campaign, according to Federal Election Commission records.

The number of self-funders who ultimately lost their elections is expected to grow in November.

Don Tracy and Barb Regnitz, the Republican nominees for U.S. Senate in Illinois and Indiana’s 1st Congressional District, respectively, each put in upward of $2 million into their campaigns so far. But both are vying for “solid” or “likely” Democratic seats and are expected to lose.

entries.title: A Big Dig
entries.content:
Good morning. This is the NOTUS Metro newsletter for Sept. 8, 2026. You can get it in your inbox every day by signing up here — it’s free!

THE LATEST

When a century-old D.C. library is standing on nothing but stilts, it can make anyone nervous.

“One wrong move by one excavator could take the whole thing down, so the stakes were literally very high,” says Jaspreet Pahwa, the director of capital planning and construction for the D.C. Public Library system.

That was one of the pitfalls of the 2 ½-year renovation of the Southeast Library in Eastern Market, which wraps up this week ahead of the library’s reopening on Thursday.

It was built in 1922 as one of the city’s three Carnegie libraries — the others are in Takoma and Mount Pleasant — so library officials had to balance protecting the historical landmark with trying to expand one of the 10 busiest neighborhood libraries in the city.

That involved digging between 24 and 40 feet under and around the building, allowing for an expansion of the ground-floor level and the addition of a basement level that will now largely serve kids. With that, the Southeast Library will double in size but leave the original historic building largely intact.

“This was a really complex project, to say the least,” says Rich Reyes-Gavilan, DCPL’s executive director. “The need was there. It was just about finding the money and the ingenuity and the know-how.”

To ensure the new basement level didn’t feel like it’s underground, a new skylight was carved from the roof down the center of the building, drawing natural light all the way into the deepest recesses of the library. Reyes-Gavilan — who has overseen the modernization of dozens of libraries in his 13 years leading DCPL — says the skylight is the library’s “architectural marvel."

And there’s more: An extension was built in what used to be an alley behind the library, connecting it to a neighboring rowhouse and allowing for a new main entrance to be constructed along South Carolina Avenue.

The renovation wasn’t cheap. The $40 million price tag is roughly double what was originally contemplated, because of both increasing construction costs and a need to comply with historic preservation rules. But library officials say they were able to leverage federal COVID recovery funds to pay for it.

The next projects for the library system include a brand-new facility in Congress Heights and another in Eckington/Edgewood. Future renovations include libraries in Chevy Chase and Shepherd Park. To Reyes-Gavilan’s relief, none of these projects is expected to be as complicated as the Southeast Library makeover.





FROM THE DISTRICT

A federal planning commission has approved the transfer of the D.C. Armory, the headquarters of the District’s National Guard, to local control, NOTUS’ Kendall Staton reports. The transfer still has to be approved by D.C.’s mayor, the D.C. Council and Congress.

D.C.’s Department of Public Works is testing rat-proof trash bins in high-traffic areas of the city, WUSA9 reports.

President Donald Trump has become obsessed with “architectural immortality” — building monuments around D.C. that will outlast him, New York Magazine reports.

Former Kennedy Center chair David Rubenstein has purchased the large sculpture that was removed from the grounds of the venue last week, The New York Times reports. Rubenstein, a billionaire philanthropist who owns the Orioles, sat as chair from 2010 to 2025, when he was ousted as part of Trump’s takeover of the center’s board. Rubenstein reportedly paid more than $2 million for the abstract sculpture, titled “Blue.”

The grieving tree: D.C. residents have been leaving condolence messages on a large tree in Dupont Circle that was severed by last week’s wild storm.





FROM MARYLAND

All aboard! The stretch of the Red Line between North Bethesda and Friendship Heights reopened Monday after nine weeks of construction work. The project finished “on time and on budget,” Metro said in a news release.





D.C. TRIVIA


Where did the first D.C. Public Library branch open in 1911?

  1. Anacostia
  2. Capitol Hill
  3. Takoma
Email us the answer — the first reader who gets it right gets a shout-out. The answer will be at the end of the newsletter tomorrow.





SPORTS

Jayden Daniels camp AP - 26238573512493 (3872x2581, AR: 1.50)
The Commanders should have plenty of bulletin board material this season. In a roundup of preseason coverage and power rankings, NOTUS’ Alex Schiffer reports that many national analysts and pundits are down on Washington ahead of a pivotal year for GM Adam Peters and coach Dan Quinn.

“Skinny quarterback who got hurt last year combined with nobody who can block?” The Ringer’s Bill Simmons said on a recent podcast. “I’m out.”

High school football season is fully underway, with Maryland public schools kicking off this past weekend. NOTUS’ Noah Ferguson highlights five standouts from around the area in our Players of the Week column; this week’s group includes a Quince Orchard DB who nabbed three interceptions and a Gonzaga running back who scored four touchdowns.

DMV native Frances Tiafoe has advanced to the quarterfinals of the U.S. Open. The 28-year-old Tiafoe, currently ranked the No. 12 men’s tennis player in the world, will face 22-year-old American Alex Michelsen today at 1 p.m. Tiafoe is chasing his first Grand Slam title.

What to Watch Today

MLB: Nationals at Padres, 9:40 p.m. (MLB.TV)

entries.title: Down in Dallas
entries.content:
Today’s notice: What’s the message out of Republicans’ midterm convention? Nearly 70 candidates have self-funded their campaigns; most lost. Democrats eye a DOGE-ish idea. And: What's happening with the screwworm scare?

THE LATEST

There's been a lot of reporting about Republicans frustrated with White House messaging — that it’s all about Donald Trump, and not about what voters care about, or at least what to tell them 56 days from the midterms. This week in Dallas, the party’s midterm convention could provide another taste of that messaging.

If last month is any preview, expect to hear about communism, liberals and how Democrats, including Joe Biden, are to blame for the current ills. Nearly 20 months into office, Trump still often mentions the former president — dropping more than a dozen references to Biden in August alone.

A White House official told NOTUS that Trump has made Biden his foil because “he’s drawing a contrast with the historic successes of his first 19 months with the Biden years.”

Former Biden White House comms strategist Andrew Bates — who’s advising multiple Democratic campaigns this cycle — says he thinks Trump’s references to his predecessor only underscore how good things were pre-Trump. Republicans “going out of their way to bring up a time when the economy was stronger and we weren’t stuck in Iran just highlights how much they’ve ripped off the American people and failed the tests they set for themselves in 2024,” he said.

Trump launched a torrent of Truth Social posts this weekend: sharing fake AI images of “Iran's Navy” on the ocean floor; claiming the moon and the Strait of Hormuz as American territory; depicting Mexico, Canada and Greenland covered in the red, white and blue; rebranding New Mexico as “New America.”

He also celebrated shiny D.C. statues and fountains, unveiled Space Force uniforms and brought George Washington to the Oval Office for a chitchat. And, of course, he posted Biden wearing a Trump 2024 cap. Those issues aren’t necessarily topping voters’ lists — It may cost me $100 to fill up my truck but dammit, have we renamed New Mexico? It could explain why so many Republicans didn’t buy a ticket to Texas.

More on NOTUS: Suspect Identified in Attack on Ohio Gubernatorial Candidate Amy Acton | Missouri Group Asks the Supreme Court to Let Former District Maps Stand | German Far-Right Party Is Projected to Win Regional Election | Trump Administration Asks the Supreme Court to Lift Block on Mail-in Voting Regulations


From the campaign trail


Self-funding and still coming up short. A record number of wealthy candidates — 69 — have so far spent more than $1 million of their own money to support their campaigns for federal office, NOTUS’ Mark Alfred reports. And as primary season ends, about two-thirds of these self-funders have already turned out to be losers. Mark spoke with some of them, and a surprisingly high number said the experience of spending millions of their own dollars just to flame out has left them hungry to run again.

From a potential future 


Democrats wanna DOGE, too. The Trump team and DOGE were “correct in identifying that people want things to work better,” Virginia Gov. Abigail Spanberger told NOTUS’ Natalie Alms. “Rather cynically, they used that sentiment to their electoral advantage, and then used it as a mandate to break things further.” She’s one of many Democrats who say there's a way to pick up the mantle Elon Musk nominally claimed — tech modernization — to showcase that liberals can make state and local governments hum. Natalie explores how some in the Democratic Party hope they’ll get the chance to unleash their own DOGE soon.


NOTUS METRO

Local news: D.C. Is on Track to Control Armory Land Near RFK Stadium, by Kendall Staton

Sports desk: National Pundits Have Low Expectations for the Commanders This Season, by Alex Schiffer

DMV High School Football Players of Week 2, by Noah Ferguson

NEW ON NOTUS

The strange case of the disappearing screwworm. The dangerous pest, discovered within the United States in June, has been targeted by the Agriculture Department with the goal of protecting cattle and other livestock herds from an infestation straight out of a horror movie. The effort was expected to take years, NOTUS’ Tyler Spence writes, but in August the USDA publicly reported that only four cases were detected, and none in cattle. Tyler writes that many people who follow the screwworm are very skeptical of this figure. “It doesn’t make a lot of sense, biologically,” a former longtime USDA official told NOTUS.

Some experts question whether the agency has the personnel and the resources to properly track and contain the screwworm, Tyler writes, and point to the significant department staff reductions from DOGE. The USDA says it’s simply very good at its job: “The low case count is a direct result of the aggressive, science-driven five-prong strategy to eradicate NWS unveiled by Secretary [Brooke] Rollins a year ago,” a spokesperson said.

entries.title: National Pundits Have Low Expectations for the Commanders This Season
entries.summary: Ahead of a pivotal year, coach Dan Quinn’s team has not received a lot of love from analysts.
entries.content:
The Commanders open a third season under coach Dan Quinn on Sunday with an afternoon matchup against the Eagles.

After a dream campaign in 2024, last year did not go to plan for Washington and the team finished 5-12. Projections for this year are wide-ranging, with a few analysts hopeful for the Commanders but many expecting a long season.

What They’re Saying

The Ringer’s Bill Simmons said on a recent podcast that the Commanders are a “lock” to finish under the 7.5 wins FanDuel has projected for the team.

Sign up for the NOTUS Metro newsletter for essential coverage of the D.C. region.

“They lost [Laremy] Tunsil for the season and I didn’t like their offensive line to begin with,” Simmons said. “If you’re reading the day-to-day reports, really rough stuff with the offensive line. Which, normally not everybody has a good offensive line — but their quarterback is 127 pounds. So the skinny quarterback who got hurt last year combined with nobody who can block? I’m out.”

ESPN analyst and former NFL quarterback Dan Orlovsky named the Commanders the league’s most confusing team in an interview with Dan Patrick on Friday. Orlovsky cited the Commanders’ busy offseason and 31-year-old David Blough as a first-time offensive coordinator among his concerns with the organization.

“What’s the offensive actually going to be?” Orlovsky said. “You lose your left tackle who you just made the highest-paid left tackle in football and all your fans are like, ‘We'll be OK.’ Those two things can't happen at the same time. … It's an unbelievably expensive defense but a little bit unproven. …”

“And so it could go really good if they gel and those high-end-paid players play at such a high level and the free agent signings and the draft picks play at such a high level. Or it could be a season of question, of, ‘OK where is this organization headed,’ and a second year of maybe some up and down from Jayden Daniels. I’m bullish on them, but I’m just not all in.”

Power Rankings 

Yahoo! Sports has the Commanders in its “work to do” category, citing player development and injury luck as two factors that could define the season.

Similarly, CBS Sports ranked the team in the C tier of its power rankings, which is for teams that could make the playoffs if everything goes right.

ESPN has the Commanders 20th in its power rankings, one spot lower than where the network ranked the team after last spring’s draft.

The Athletic recently ranked the Commanders 13th of the 16 teams in its NFC power ranking and put Washington 23rd in its league ranking before training camp. The NFC ranking was conducted with multiple team executives weighing in. One executive told The Athletic that a healthy Daniels is enough to make up for the numerous question marks surrounding the team.

"They get Jayden back, and Terry McLaurin will be healthy," the executive told The Athletic. "They've added some really good parts defensively in free agency. They have to get the offensive line solidified."

Another executive was much less optimistic.

"I think they are going to be bad," they said. "The quarterback is talented, but his style of play, unless he changes it, is a concern. The weapons around him are OK, but I don't think it's a dynamic team offensively. Defensively, they plateaued."

Long odds

The sportsbooks have a similar take, giving Washington long odds to make a real impact this season. On Monday at FanDuel, the Commanders were (+265) to make the playoffs, (+550) to win the division and (+6500) to win the Super Bowl. The odds at DraftKings are similar. Essentially, the books think the Commanders have less than a 30% chance to make the playoffs.

entries.title: Democrats Are Plotting Government Efficiency in a Post-DOGE World
entries.summary: Rising stars in the Democratic Party are promoting their tech modernization teams in a post-DOGE political landscape.
entries.content:
New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani made a big show of bringing his “pothole politics” online: He donned his sunglasses, lowered himself into a go-kart and took a lap around a track in Coney Island to sell his new Public Interest Technology Crew, or PIT Crew. (Get it?)

The team’s mission is to make the city’s clunky online systems easier to use and to help enact his agenda. It’s an initiative Democrats are adopting across the country. In Virginia, Gov. Abigail Spanberger, too, is setting up a crew of tech whizzes to bring government services into the 21st century.

Many of the people running those teams are alumni of the U.S. Digital Service, the relatively unknown Obama-era tech squad that President Donald Trump transformed into DOGE on Day 1 of his second administration.

Now, they’re out of Washington and working for some of the rising stars of the Democratic Party who want to use technology to enact the liberal agenda and show voters that they can get things done.

“What I heard along the campaign trail, and certainly now that I’ve been governor, is people have this sense that things don’t work,” Spanberger told NOTUS in an interview.

The Trump team and DOGE were “correct in identifying that people want things to work better,” she said. “Rather cynically, they used that sentiment to their electoral advantage, and then used it as a mandate to break things further.”

More than 10 blue states have digital services teams — many of them with former U.S. Digital Service staffers and several of them established before the second Trump administration. Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro set up a digital team in 2023. Maryland Gov. Wes Moore, in 2024. By comparison, only two red states have similar units.

The teams are an answer to what Donald Moynihan, a public policy professor at the University of Michigan, calls a progressive “neuroses” that wants to prove liberals can govern effectively, part of a movement calling for “abundance” — more development, more ambitious policies, faster.

That, and the national focus on DOGE, have brought what was once a relatively behind-the-scenes administrative effort, like building a website, into the foreground.

“Doing the good work is the core of what we need to do every day,” said Luke Farrell, a deputy commissioner and senior adviser for the New York City government. “But also, we then need to show people the work, and we need to get it into people’s hands.”

Mamdani’s PIT Crew has been tasked with making his administration’s “click-to-cancel” rule into a reality with an online portal for New Yorkers to file complaints. The consumer protection rule, which requires businesses to provide simple subscription cancellation, is projected to save New Yorkers millions of dollars once it goes into effect next month.

In Virginia, the digital team is being told to address the inefficiencies that disrupt the daily lives of residents; Virginians still have to write checks to the state because they can’t pay for some state services online, Spanberger said. Other parts of the state government still require traditional signatures.

“One of the ways that you can best ensure that you're correctly utilizing state taxpayer dollars is to make things actually work,” Spanberger said. “The state digital service is meant to be a part of that.”
Abigail Spanberger AP-23311573084272 (4411x2941, AR: 1.50)President Barack Obama set up the U.S. Digital Service in 2014 to fix HealthCare.gov after a botched rollout threatened to tank Obamacare, one of the Obama administration’s signature policies. The unit became a core part of a network of tech do-gooders in the federal government.

After the HealthCare.gov rescue, the team largely operated in the background of government. During the first Trump administration, the leadership of the U.S. Digital Service fashioned the team as a nonpartisan unit. In a shift, the Biden administration installed political leadership and tasked it with working on priorities like building a government program to file federal taxes for free.

Still, when Trump returned to office, few Americans were familiar with the tech team that the president and Elon Musk transformed into DOGE.

In the early months of the second Trump administration, many of the existing U.S. Digital Service staffers were laid off. Others resigned publicly, saying that DOGE’s work was antithetical to the mission of the original team. 18F, another Obama-era government tech team, was shuttered in March 2025, weeks after Musk tweeted that it had been “deleted.”

DOGE quickly departed from its nominal tech focus to overhaul of the federal workforce and slash government spending — moves that inspired nationwide protests and lawsuits. The backlash has given Democrats nationally an opportunity to reclaim the government efficiency mantle.

That conversation has already begun in Washington. Liberal think tanks and former federal officials are drafting plans for how future administrations could improve the government, as NOTUS has previously reported. The work could have an impact beyond political resonance: In New York, Virginia and the capital alike, these efforts to improve technology and government could help politicians actually implement their agendas.

“A policy without a way to enforce it isn’t really a policy at all,” Erie Meyer, who was previously the chief technologist at the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau, told NOTUS of the importance of the PIT Crew’s work implementing Mamdani’s click-to-cancel rule.

Mamdani’s team is still deciding on what other projects they’ll focus on, but the work will be “core to the Mamdani administration's agenda around affordability, housing, consumer and worker protection and more,” said Maya Israni, senior adviser to the city’s chief technology officer.

More than 4,000 people have submitted applications to join the New York City PIT crews, which will consist of five teams focusing on building services in-house instead of using contractors.

“We really want to have a direct impact on someone’s day-to-day life as a New Yorker and make their life on a day-to-day basis better and more affordable,” Israni said. “We’re here to deliver on core Mamdani administration priorities.”

At the state level, Democrats are also using the teams to respond to Trump’s agenda. Spanberger said Virginia’s tech push is especially relevant in light of the Republican budget law passed last year, which slashed federal funding in food assistance programs and Medicaid.

As the state implements Medicaid work requirements from that law, how well various state systems interface to validate eligibility becomes really important, said Spanberger, noting that “any of those gaps means loss of coverage or means loss of social safety net programs for people in a way that can really be harmful.”

The tension: Sometimes the work to enable policies isn’t flashy.

The goal of the new tech unit in Virginia is to “improve the services that the government provides for every Virginian,” Andrea Fletcher — who also previously worked in the U.S. Digital Service and just recently started as the new director of the Virginia Digital Service — told NOTUS.

To do that, the Virginia team will also be looking to tackle the “boring stuff” that often makes the government headache-inducing in the first place, like procurement and hiring, she said.

During DOGE’s heyday in Washington, some who had previously been on civic tech teams in Washington expressed envy at the political aircover Elon Musk’s team had to get things done.

The teams in New York and Virginia have that top-down investment, said Lynn Overmann, who worked as a senior adviser for the Biden administration as part of the U.S. Digital Service.

The real test, she said: “Can they actually get it done?”

entries.title: Screwworm Cases Are Going Down. Experts Are Suspicious.
entries.summary: “It doesn’t make a lot of sense, biologically,” a former longtime USDA official said.
entries.content:
America’s fight against the New World screwworm was expected to be a multiyear effort, yet the number of new cases has dropped to a surprisingly low level.

Only four cases of screwworm were detected in the U.S. in August and none of them in cattle, according to a dashboard maintained by the Agriculture Department. In June, there had been 30 cases detected, and an expectation that the fight against the screwworm had a long way to go.

That August number baffles experts, given how far the screwworm had advanced into Texas and the high number of cases in Mexico and Central America.

“It’s very strange,” a former longtime USDA official who worked for the department’s plant and animal health department told NOTUS. “It doesn’t make a lot of sense, biologically.”

On top of that, the USDA reports it hasn’t detected screwworm through trapping flies or seeing the pest in any wildlife or feral animals, the primary ways officials might expect to keep tabs on the population and their movement.

“Zero cases in wildlife is unexplainable to me,” Texas Agriculture Commissioner Sid Miller told NOTUS. Miller said that he and horticulturists on his team have caught what they believed to be screwworm in traps, only to have the tests come back negative when sent to the USDA.

One current employee at the USDA’s Animal and Plant Health Inspection Service called the lack of cases in traps or wildlife “suspicious,” saying, “It doesn’t seem very likely to me that we haven’t trapped a single wild fly.”

The USDA says its playbook for fighting screwworm is working, which is why cases are so low. The New World screwworm is a fly that feeds on living tissue in animals and even humans. The infestation can be lethal to animals if left untreated and is considered a major threat to livestock in warm climates.

“The low case count is a direct result of the aggressive, science-driven five-prong strategy to eradicate NWS unveiled by Secretary [Brooke] Rollins a year ago,” a spokesperson for the USDA said in a statement. “This strategy, led by USDA and other federal partners, has increased tracking of the fly’s movement, inspections of impacted animals both wild and domestic, and substantially built up sterile fly capability through coordination with states and industry.”

The agency reopened the port of Douglas, Arizona, to livestock after more than a year of movement restrictions aimed at keeping the screwworm out of the U.S. The USDA conducts inspections of the livestock at the border and said it plans to reopen additional ports if successful in Douglas.

The agency also lifted movement restrictions on three counties this week ,two in Texas and one in New Mexico.

The USDA said on X that it has released 1 billion sterile flies, or male flies that mate with females but don’t produce offspring and effectively stop the lifecycle over time. Rollins and Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin wrote an op-ed Friday touting their efforts.

At the beginning of the summer, Rollins acknowledged that the agency needed 400 million more sterile flies a week to effectively combat the screwworm, a number that would likely take several months or a year to reach.

In the meantime, cases across Mexico and Central America have reached over 200,000, with 500 human cases in Mexico alone.

Some experts question whether the agency has the personnel and the resources to properly track and contain the screwworm. The USDA has undergone significant staffing reductions to many of its departments since the start of the second Trump administration.

“The critical mass is just not there to do the work that needs to be done,” the former USDA manager said.

And some former USDA officials question whether the current surveillance methods are working or whether screwworm is truly being contained effectively. “They're using wildlife cameras to do surveillance, and USDA is claiming that it works well, but it's also not catching anything,” a former USDA official who oversaw screwworm response told NOTUS.

Miller also raised doubts over the ability for cameras to identify open wounds and screwworm on animals, saying he has seen the video the cameras produce himself. “It’s not the best videos,” Miller said. He said the videos are fine for identifying animals, but are not the same as a medical examination.

The USDA said that the footage from these cameras is reviewed by wildlife biologists, with assistance from AI tools to identify animals with wounds.

Experts are also concerned that the current system does not incentivize ranchers to report cases. Current rules require cattle ranchers to keep their herds in quarantined areas, which can cause ranchers to lose money without any indemnity in return from the USDA.

Both former USDA officials said the USDA set up an indemnity program during the bird flu outbreaks beginning in 2024, something that has not been done for cattle ranchers with screwworm.

Both the current and former APHIS employees echoed this concern, saying ranchers would be uninterested in self-reporting due to concerns over movement restrictions or government surveillance.

The USDA said the agency provides indemnity for any animal that must be culled to prevent the spread of disease or parasites.

The U.S. eradication campaign that eventually beat back screwworm in the 20th century took the better part of a decade of sustained effort. USDA formally launched its sterile insect technique program across the southeastern U.S. in 1957. Florida was declared screwworm-free by 1958, and a large-scale push into Texas began in 1962, with ranchers reporting screwworm-free herds for the first time in modern memory by 1963. The U.S. wasn't declared fully free of the pest until 1966 — nine years after the campaign began in earnest.

Even then, the win proved fragile, with a resurgence tied to reinfestation from Mexico in 1972. Even after the 1966 declaration, eradication pushed steadily south over the following decades, with Mexico declared screwworm-free in 1991 and Belize, Guatemala, Honduras and El Salvador following through the mid-1990s.

“I think it's still too early to tell what the situation is with the flies,” the current APHIS employee said before expressing optimism that screwworm has been defeated once and can be defeated again; it’s “just a matter of how much time and money it will take.”

entries.title: Canada Strikes Back With Tariffs on U.S. Goods
entries.summary: The tariffs hit hundreds of American products.
entries.content:
Canada struck back at Trump on Tuesday with tariffs on about $20 billion worth of U.S. goods, in response to the latest round of tariffs on Canada.

The outcome could resonate far beyond Canada, showing other governments whether a smaller U.S. ally can withstand Trump’s economic pressure.

Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney says U.S. demands could hollow out key Canadian industries and limit the country’s independence, and Trump’s threats to Canadian sovereignty have rallied the public behind him.

“Carney and Canada have become symbolic of resistance to him,” Canadian historian Robert Bothwell said. “And what he’ll want to do is make an example of Carney and Canada and theoretically terrify everybody else while in fact showing them that they need to remove themselves even further from the United States.”

The tariffs hit hundreds of American products, including steel, aluminum, cheese, appliances, clothing, cosmetics and farm equipment, at rates of 15%, 25% or 50%.

entries.title: Trump Is Quietly Planning to Majorly Change How National Parks Are Run
entries.summary: All Interior Department bureaus are considering major shake-ups under an edict from leadership.
entries.content:
The Trump administration is planning to significantly reorganize the National Park Service and other bureaus of the Interior Department, the second major shake-up of the nation’s public lands infrastructure in less than two years.

The agency is looking to reshape its most public-facing offices, according to draft internal agency planning documents from late August obtained by NOTUS and confirmed by an Interior executive involved in the reorganizations who spoke on the condition of anonymity.

The reorganization plans across Interior were developed in a “very hush hush” manner,” the executive said, noting that no one aside from the very top leadership of each subagency has been involved in the discussions. That secrecy has created a culture of fear and anxiety in the agency and among National Park advocates, who have been cautioning against another reorganization, as NOTUS reported last week.

The Interior Department has already lost more than 10,000 employees since President Donald Trump retook office, largely through voluntary resignation programs directed by Interior Secretary Doug Burgum and the White House. Last year’s reorganization moved support staff into Burgum’s office.

In its draft documents, NPS said that it anticipated it would avoid layoffs “in the short term,” but in prepared talking points tells officials to “avoid categorical promises; explain notification process” if asked about staff reductions.

The country’s 430 park units would experience a significant change under the proposed plans. The documents describe transitioning the park service to a new “hub and spoke” model, with some “hub” parks given the power to manage priorities, leadership and direction for “spoke” parks that would report them, according to the documents.

Currently park superintendents report to regional leadership. While the regional system will remain in place, the draft documents indicate that Interior intends for power to be centralized in the “hub” parks: They would direct priorities and vision, while “spoke” parks would be responsible for implementation.

The documents also indicate that the park service intends for resources to be shared more widely between the spoke and hub parks, with the hub carrying more responsibility for the management of those resources. (The draft plans included a visual representation of the reorganization created with Anthropic’s Claude AI tool, according to an internal note in one of the documents.)

The new organization is intended to “build a more efficient and effective operation, optimize resource sharing across parks and programs, and enhance accountability and supervision,” the draft documents read.

The Interior Department did not respond to a request for comment.

Details of the plan are still subject to change, according to the documents and people familiar with the plans. The Interior executive said last week a career official overseeing the effort introduced a new framework for bureaus to use to rearrange themselves. Previous deadlines were pushed back or removed altogether.

Rachel Borra, Interior’s human resources chief, who previously helped spearhead layoffs at the department last fall that were ultimately blocked in federal court, has been meeting with management in recent weeks to go over details of the various “realignments,” according to documents reviewed by NOTUS. She is scheduled to hold a progress meeting on realignment efforts on Tuesday.

Changes at National Parks could have disparate impacts, where functions range from the preservation of natural wonders in Yellowstone to the protection of rare ecosystems in Channel Islands to the preservation of historical and cultural memory at Valley Forge. While currently superintendents are largely responsible for ensuring that mission is met within their individual park, the new structure appears to centralize some management with the “hub” superintendent.

That centralization could come at the cost of each individual park’s needs, former officials said.

“It’s remarkable from A to Z how different units in the National Park Service are and how they have to adapt to location conditions, and that can drive people in D.C. crazy because they really like it when everything fits in neat boxes,” said Jeff Mow, the former superintendent of Glacier National Park and a 40-year veteran of the Park Service. “And there’s a whole lot about the National Park Service that doesn't fit into neat boxes.”

“Any time you see these top-down initiatives come through — almost never in my career did I ever see one that can encompass the diversity within the organization,” he continued.

Russell Galipeau, who served as superintendent of Channel Islands National Park for 15 years, said that it is already difficult for the country’s smaller and lesser-known parks to advocate on behalf of their needs and priorities.

“We want to reorganize. We want to make things more efficient. You know what? We can do all those things, but how is that actually helping us be a leader and setting an example of how we protect our nation's natural and cultural resources?” he asked.

The draft documents detailing the agency’s reorganization plans were not meant to be made public and stress the importance of delivering information to employees and stakeholders on the department’s own timeline.

While Interior in its internal communications insisted its plans represented common-sense solutions, declining to fully rule out layoffs, phrasing such as “reducing duplication” and demands that supervisors “not speculate about effects on specific employees,” coupled with previous efforts to slash staff and ongoing hiring restrictions, are likely to have staff and public lands advocates on edge about the administration’s intentions.

“National parks do not operate in a bubble, they are intrinsic parts of local communities. And if this proposed reorganization plan moves forward, it is going to jeopardize park relationships with communities, stakeholders, and partners,” said Emily Thompson, the executive director of the Coalition to Protect America’s National Parks.
America 250 Trump Roosevelt Library (4104x2736, AR: 1.50)The documents also lay out details of how individual offices within NPS are set to be restructured. The agency tentatively plans to remake its culture and science division into an office called Resource Stewardship. Employees have raised concerns that the administration would seek to de-emphasize its scientific and cultural work. A new Law Enforcement, Safety and Health Division would replace a Visitor and Resource Protection office.

The agency has been planning how to announce this reorganization since July 2026 but has not yet notified Congress of its intention to reorganize, according to the documents and a Senate aide. The Interior Department is legally obligated to notify Congress of any planned reorganization.

The secrecy of these plans have frustrated advocates, former officials and current staffers alike.

“This reorganization could fundamentally change how our national parks operate, without any clear communication about what ‘problem’ might be solved. It can't possibly be addressing budgets or efficiency,” Thompson said. “There are going to be countless issues and challenges involving park funding, travel and other logistics — this will waste taxpayer dollars and further contribute to the chaos that already exists.”

The implementation of the plan has already changed in at least one regard from the schedule laid out in documents obtained by NOTUS: While planning meetings were scheduled with senior officials for this week and superintendents for the middle of September, those meetings have been canceled, according to multiple sources familiar with the change. NPS planned to begin implementing the changes this year, though it is not clear if that timeline remains operative.

The Interior Department intensified its reorganization process in early 2026, with upper management telling leadership at each bureau that the dramatic staffing reductions opened the door to rethink how they are organized. At least at some bureaus, internal leadership maintained autonomy in developing plans and new organizational structures. They then worked with the Office of Personnel Management on implementation of those ideas.

Department officials made clear to individual bureau leadership that “This is the time to take a big swing,” the Interior executive said.

While Interior was on the verge of laying off thousands of employees at multiple points last year, they never took effect due to various court orders. The department still successfully upended some parts of its workforce. Last month, top agency officials reassigned more than two dozen of its top career executives, requiring many people to move into new jobs with limited relationship to their background and expertise.

The Park Service has already been “bleeding,” both because Burgum directed national park resources toward D.C. beautification efforts and because of last year’s reorganization, said one current employee. Bureaus across Interior are still paying Burgum’s office to house employees it subsumed as part of that reorganization, employees said.

Through the renewed reorganization efforts, Burgum is continuing to exert his influence over the shape of the department. He has already merged the Bureau of Ocean Energy Management and Bureau of Safety and Environmental Enforcement, undoing a change under former President Barack Obama. The secretary has also merged all the department’s firefighters into a new component over some bipartisan reservations from Congress.

Between those changes and the staffing losses from the Trump administration’s push to reduce the federal workforce, advocates are already concerned what another round of changes will portend.

“We find a way to say it's more efficient, and what we end up doing is finding out we have less and less resources to work with,” Galipeau said.

“Perhaps reorganization wouldn’t be necessary if these unnecessary cuts weren’t made.”

entries.title: Trump Threatens Canadian Jetmaker With Extensive U.S. Footprint
entries.summary: Bombardier has a significant presence is Kansas, which Trump won by about 16 percentage points in 2024.
entries.content:
U.S. President Donald Trump has threatened to ban the sale of aircraft from Canada’s Bombardier unless it manufactures planes in the United States.

In response, the maker of private jets noted that many components for its planes, including the wings, are produced in the U.S. and its supply chain relies heavily on U.S. companies.

Since Canada-U.S. trade talks collapsed on Aug. 21, Trump and his administration have unleashed a barrage of tariffs, threats and personal attacks portraying Canada as weak and dependent. Canada retaliated Tuesday with tariffs on about $20 billion worth of U.S. goods.

“NO MORE SELLING BOMBARDIER IN THE UNITED STATES! Their products aren’t good enough!” Trump said in a Monday social media post. “If they want our Market, they must build here, and stop treating America like a ‘piggybank.’”

Bombardier said in a statement that the American aerospace industry is a “clear winner on trade and exports.” It said it creates tens of thousands of jobs both directly and through its supply chain.

Bombardier's supply chain includes about 2,800 U.S. companies in 47 states, it said. Among other things, wings for its business jets are made in Texas and flight control components are produced near Los Angeles.

“Bombardier values its great partnership with American companies and its U.S. employees. Our plan is to continue to invest in our people, our customers, and the communities in which we operate across the country,” it said.

One state where Bombardier has a significant presence is Kansas, which Trump won by about 16 percentage points in 2024.

U.S. Sen. Jerry Moran of Kansas said in a social media post Monday that Bombardier supports a local workforce of more than 1,000 Kansans.

“I reached out to the Trump administration to make certain the President is aware of the significant contributions of Bombardier to Kansas and the importance of its presence in Wichita to many Kansas workers at Bombardier and in the Bombardier supply chain,” Moran wrote in his post.

Moran promised to continued working to ensure that the planemaker's manufacturing operations remain in Kansas.

Earlier this year, Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney announced that his government will buy six early warning radar planes from Sweden’s Saab and Bombardier, rather than from U.S. aircraft makers. The Saab planes use Bombardier’s Global 6500 aircraft platform, supporting Canadian manufacturing. They have 20% U.S. content. The alternatives would have been U.S.-made E-7A Wedgetail surveillance aircraft made by Boeing or the Aeris X, made by L3Harris.

The Canadian government is reviewing plans to buy U.S. F-35 fighter jets. Saab has proposed making its Gripen fighter jet in Canada.

Bombardier is one of Canada's oldest and most well-known manufacturers. The company was founded by Joseph-Armand Bombardier, an inventor and entrepreneur in Canada’s rural Quebec who started out making snowmobiles and other snow-going equipment in the 1930s.

Over its long history, it entered and left the train-making business and expanded for a time into making regional and commercial aircraft. But it sold off those parts of its business as it restructured to focus on making private business jets.

The company also has spun off parts of its business making snowmobiles and other recreational equipment.

entries.title: Iceland Summons U.S. Ambassador for a Rebuke Over Trump’s Truth Social Post
entries.summary: Billy Long had been forced to apologize for an earlier joke he made calling Iceland the “52nd state.”
entries.content:
The U.S. ambassador to Iceland, Billy Long, was summoned by the country’s officials for a meeting on Monday just hours after President Donald Trump posted an image to Truth Social of the Arctic nation blanketed in the American flag.

Trump posted a stylized map of North and Central American nations — including Canada, the U.S., Mexico, Greenland and Iceland — covered in the stars and stripes during a posting spree to Truth Social on Sunday, an apparent indication of his interest in taking control of those countries. Trump also shared a bizarre series of AI-generated images of “Iran's Navy” on the ocean floor, the moon and the Strait of Hormuz as American territories and New Mexico renamed “New America.”

The posts caught the attention of Icelandic officials, who have tangled with the Trump administration since the president returned to office last year.

"It was made clear to him in the meeting that the post was entirely unacceptable," Iceland's Minister for Foreign Affairs Þorgerður Katrín Gunnarsdóttir told broadcaster RÚV of her meeting with Long.

“If this is supposed to be a joke, then it is a bad joke,” she added at a press conference Tuesday, according to Arctic Today.

This isn’t the first time that Long has faced scrutiny over U.S. annexation threats. Long apologized before the Senate Foreign Relations Committee in February over a joke he made, first reported by Politico, to former House colleagues calling Iceland the “52nd state” and saying he’d serve as its governor.

“It was totally inappropriate,” Long told senators at the time. “I just hope that the people in Iceland will give me a second chance to make a first impression.”

Icelanders launched a petition earlier this year calling for Gunnarsdóttir to oust Long, with the effort garnering nearly 5,500 signatures.

Long joins a group of other Trump-tapped ambassadors who have faced removal campaigns and diplomatic rebukes.

Pete Hoekstra, the U.S. ambassador to Canada, currently faces a removal petition that has accumulated nearly 270,000 signatures — an outgrowth of the escalating U.S.-Canada trade war.

Bill White, the U.S. ambassador to Belgium, has been summoned by the country’s officials twice this year — most recently to answer for an incendiary social media post in which he mocked the country’s health minister.

Trump’s post of an American flag-covered map has renewed fears in the region of a potential U.S. annexation of Iceland's close neighbor, Greenland.

Shortly after the start of his second term, Trump pushed for the U.S. to take control of Greenland. Last January, the president even said that conversations with NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte at the World Economic Forum in Davos, Switzerland, had generated “the framework of a future deal” on Greenland.

Trump maintains that Greenland, which is a Danish territory, is vital for U.S. national security, but the push has landed with a thud in Europe — particularly in Denmark, which launched massive protests in response to the president’s push for control in the Arctic.

Iceland also joined Denmark, Finland, Iceland, Norway and Sweden in a joint statement in January defending Greenland from Trump's annexation threats.

“We collectively reiterate that matters concerning Denmark and Greenland are for Denmark and Greenland to decide alone,” the foreign ministers of each country wrote.
entries.author: Jenna Monnin

entries.title: Trump Administration Removes Criticism of Confederate Memorial From Arlington Cemetery
entries.summary: A marker at the memorial’s former site no longer says it provided a “mythologized” vision of the Confederacy.
entries.content:
The Trump administration censored language criticizing a monument to the Confederacy that previously stood at Arlington National Cemetery, removing a reference to the memorial’s “nostalgic, mythologized vision.”

The bronze statue depicting Confederate soldiers alongside enslaved people stood for more than a century before being removed in 2023 as part of a congressional mandate to remove symbols honoring the Confederacy on U.S. military property. The cemetery’s website described the memorial as showing “a nostalgic, mythologized vision of the Confederacy, including highly sanitized depictions of slavery.”

That language, along with further explanation of how history has “denied the horrors of slavery,” has been scrubbed ahead of a planned reinstallment next year. A marker at the former memorial site has also been replaced, with the new version missing any mention of slavery.

Last year, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said in a social media post announcing the return of the statue that it should never have been taken down.

“Unlike the Left, we don’t believe in erasing American history — we honor it,” he wrote.

Hegseth referred to the statue as “The Reconciliation Monument.” Historian Karen Cox said the language removed from the website was “absolutely accurate” historical context around the statue, which plays into the false idea that the South didn’t fight the Civil War to keep slavery but rather to protect states’ rights.

“Built into that narrative are lies,” she said. “It’s an attempt by the South to justify the confederacy, justify its role in the war and provide this gauzy haze over the Old South and slavery.”

Cox said the statue has been drawn into the GOP culture war as the Trump administration pushes back on what it calls “woke history” and attacks the discipline as a whole.

The Defense Department directed questions to Arlington National Cemetery, which did not immediately respond Tuesday.

President Donald Trump has ordered the revision of multiple exhibits and descriptions of slavery and racism since his return to the White House as part of an effort to remove references to “corrosive ideology.” From Boston’s Bunker Hill to Washington’s Smithsonian institutions, discussions of race have been altered, removed or censored.

The debate over Confederate statues heated up in 2015 after a shooting killed nine congregation members at Emanuel African Methodist Episcopal Church, a historically Black church in Charleston, South Carolina. After protests across the U.S., some cities began removing statues that honored Confederate soldiers and generals. Almost 150 statues were removed between 2015 and 2020.

Trump has worked to replace some of them, including a sculpture of Confederate Gen. Albert Pike that stood in D.C.’s Judiciary Square until 2020 when protestors tore it down and set it on fire. The statue was re-erected last year, and is the only outdoor monument in D.C. to honor a Confederate general.
entries.author: Kendall Staton

entries.title: Smithsonian Head Announces His Retirement After Months of Criticism From Trump
entries.summary: Lonnie Bunch III will retire at the end of 2026, wrapping up a nearly eight-year tenure as the institution’s leader.
entries.content:
Smithsonian Secretary Lonnie Bunch III announced Tuesday that he will retire at the end of the year, wrapping up a nearly eight-year tenure as the institution’s leader.

His departure comes as the Smithsonian faces mounting pressure from the Trump administration over how it tells American history. In an interview with The New York Times, Bunch said it was not the pressure from the White House that led to his departure, but that the back-and-forth did take a toll on him.

“I have to be honest, it has been stressful,” he told the Times. “And at a certain point, I’d like to wake up in the morning and not look at my cellphone.”

Sign up for the NOTUS Metro newsletter for essential coverage of the D.C. region.

His departure comes at a consequential moment for the Smithsonian. The Trump administration has spent more than a year criticizing the institutions’ exhibits and scholarship — pushing for a more patriotic telling of American history that focuses less on divisive issues.

Bunch has resisted that pressure, while arguing that the Smithsonian’s job is to present history in all its complexity.

“Every day, I have somebody talk to me about how important it is to have complexity and nuance,” Bunch said earlier this year. He said visitors often come away from Smithsonian exhibitions understanding something they had not known before.

Chief Justice John Roberts, the chancellor of the Smithsonian, said in a statement that Bunch had “pursued excellence in the telling of our nation’s story.”

But President Donald Trump and his top officials have struck a different tune. In March, the president released an executive order critiquing the National Museum of African American History and Culture and the Smithsonian American Women’s History Museum, among other institutions, for “a concerted and widespread effort to rewrite our Nation’s history.” 

Last month, Trump also issued another order titled “Restoring Trust in the Smithsonian,” in which he says leadership of the institution “cannot be trusted to tell America’s story with honesty and gratitude.” 

The executive order came after a White House report on the Smithsonian’s National Museum of American History that argued the museum has shifted from presenting a balanced, patriotic account of U.S. history toward what the authors characterize as progressive political activism. 

As evidence, they cited curators’ emphasis on racism, oppression and inequality while minimizing America’s founders and their achievements. The report called for the museum to return to a more “unifying” presentation of American history.

Bunch pushed back against the report, sending out a memo to Smithsonian staff in which he said that the report was not a fair representation of the museum's work and the complexity of American history. 

“While there will always be room for improvement, this report is not a fair characterization of the work and totality of the National Museum of American History," Bunch said in the memo. “We remain focused on what grounds us: a steadfast commitment to scholarship, nonpartisanship, independence, accuracy, and integrity.”
entries.author: Torrie Herrington

entries.title: Pritzker Jumps Into Midterms Money Battle With New $20M PAC
entries.summary: Pritzker, a potential 2028 Democratic presidential contender, plans to target Ohio’s Rep. Max Miller and Texas’ Brandon Herrera with ad buys.
entries.content:
Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker launched a new political action committee over the weekend that plans to funnel millions of dollars into Democratic House races ahead of the midterms.

Pritzker’s Ready for the Fight PAC — a phrase often used by the governor and repeated liberally in the committee’s first ad spot — plans to invest at least $20 million in what it considers to be overlooked and competitive races, according to Politico, which reported first on the spending push.

The committee will soon target what it deems “the worst of the worst MAGA Republicans,” with ad reservations against Rep. Max Miller (R-Ohio), who’s facing allegations of domestic abuse, and Texas’ Brandon Herrera, an incendiary internet personality who specializes in firearms and calls himself the “AK Guy.”

Both Ohio’s 7th Congressional District and Texas’ 23rd Congressional District lean red, but Pritzker sees them as potential wins for Democrats — with Trump’s approval rating dropping to record lows and midterm elections historically fairing well for the party that doesn't control the White House.

“As the affordability crisis continues, Democrats must think big and take the fight to every corner to support candidates in often-overlooked races,” a press release on the PAC reads. “With everything we care about on the line, Democrats cannot retreat to a handful of battleground races.”

The governor is seen as a potential 2028 presidential contender for Democrats and often stands in strong opposition to President Donald Trump and his policies.

This week, Pritzker will be in Dallas with other Democrats to counter the inaugural GOP midterm convention, according to CNN.

In August 2025, Pritzker hosted a group of Texas lawmakers who fled the state to oppose a Trump-backed redistricting effort. Pritzker has also fought back against Trump’s tariffs that affect the Illinois soybean industry and has lambasted the president’s immigration policies.

Pritzker is running for his third term as Illinois governor, and this PAC will bring his fight against Trump’s agenda to the national stage ahead of the midterms — and a potential presidential run.

“Since launching his campaign in 2017, Gov. Pritzker has closed his speeches with the same question: are you ready for the fight? As Gov. Pritzker has proven in Illinois, Democrats can aggressively fight Trump’s dangerous agenda and deliver real results for working families,” the press release reads.
entries.author: Jenna Monnin

entries.title: U.S. Hits Iran's Aviation Industry With Crippling Sanctions
entries.summary: The Trump administration accused the 36 entities targeted this week of supporting the Islamic Republic's efforts to use its aviation sector to move weapons, personnel, and illicit cargo.
entries.content:
By Farnoush Amiri

The Trump administration on Tuesday imposed sanctions on additional aspects of Iran's aviation industry, targeting more than two dozen commercial and private airlines as well as foreign cargo service providers in its new push to isolate Tehran from its remaining trading partners.



The latest actions are part of the Trump administration’s Operation Economic Outcast campaign that is aimed at severing “critical financial lifelines” for the already heavily sanctioned Iranian government. The new penalties are focused on the remaining facets of Tehran's already beleaguered aviation ecosystem, which has been under countless sanctions from Washington for years.



“Let this be a warning to anyone doing business with Iran’s remaining airlines, all of which we sanctioned today: You are at risk of being cut off from the global financial system,” Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said in a press release.



The Trump administration accused the 36 entities targeted this week of supporting the Islamic Republic's efforts to use its aviation sector to move weapons, personnel, and illicit cargo.



It also claimed that private entities based in Turkey, the United Arab Emirates, Kazakhstan and Malaysia have provided parts and logistics services to Iran’s Mahan Air. The airline has been subject to U.S. counterterrorism sanctions since 2019 for its support for Iran’s paramilitary Revolutionary Guard, which the State Department has designated a foreign terrorist organization.
entries.author: Associated Press

entries.title: Air Force Base to Allow Religious Greetings After Hegseth Vowed to Intervene
entries.summary: A spokesperson for Kirtland Air Force Base defended the use of greetings like “have a blessed day” after a religious freedom group denounced the practice.
entries.content:
Guards at a New Mexico Air Force base were cleared to continue using religious greetings while operating the facility’s gates, according to a statement provided to NOTUS — a policy that comes after complaints about the greetings spurred Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth to defend the Christian service members.

The Military Religious Freedom Foundation, a nonprofit that advocates for the separation of church and state within the military, last week reported receiving dozens of complaints regarding guards saying “Have a blessed day” or “God bless you” to people arriving at the base’s gates.

But after the headline-grabbing criticism, a spokesperson for Kirtland Air Force Base said there were no plans to police the “common phrases” that service members use to greet each other and visitors to the facility.

“Base officials have reviewed the feedback received from a small percentage of individuals with base access and, in line with Department of the Air Force policies and the law, have not issued, and have no plans to issue, any changes to procedures either mandating or restricting the use of common phrases while welcoming personnel to the installation,” base officials told NOTUS.

Kirtland base officials added that gate guards are “expected to communicate professionally and courteously” with everyone entering the facility.

Mikey Weinstein, a former Air Force captain who founded the Military Religious Freedom Foundation, told NOTUS that he did not receive a faith-based greeting when he visited the base on Monday — though he said he heard a secondhand account of the religious greetings continuing this week.

Mandatory Air Force policy requires leaders and service members to “ensure their words and actions do not discriminate against any individual or group because of their faith, belief, or absence of belief, or extend preferential treatment for the same.”

If the religious greetings continue at the base, Weinstein said his group will pursue a writ of mandamus in federal court, which is an official court order that would require the Defense Department to follow its own regulations.

Hegseth sharply criticized the Military Religious Freedom Foundation last week and promised to intervene to protect the Christian greetings.

“The MRFF is a radical anti-Christian, pro-atheist group that attacks any/all faith inside the @DeptofWar,” Hegseth wrote Friday on X. “We will never cave to them. The @usairforce will confront this.”

Air Force Chief of Staff Gen. Kenneth Wilsbach said Friday the policies on the greetings “are unchanged,” and there were no plans to restrict “the use of common greetings while entering our bases.”

The Department of Defense did not respond to a request for comment.

Weinstein called the religious greetings a “blatant violation” of Air Force regulations that threaten religious freedoms for all military members.

“When differences become divisions, you destroy the unity, morale, discipline, and good order that are the compelling governmental interests that our U.S. Supreme Court talks about when it comes to the First Amendment in the military,” Weinstein said.

entries.title: New Grand Jury Subpoenas Sent in Trump-Russia Conspiracy Probe
entries.summary: The Justice Department is demanding testimony for an investigation into the intelligence community.
entries.content:
By Eric Tucker

The Justice Department is demanding testimony before a Florida grand jury in an investigation aiming to establish an intelligence community conspiracy against President Donald Trump, according to multiple people familiar with the matter.

New subpoenas being issued to former government officials represent an escalation in the year-long investigation as the Justice Department pursues a loosely defined theory that members of the intelligence community who scrutinized Trump over the last decade, including over Russian interference in the 2016 election, conspired against him and violated his rights.

Investigators in recent days contacted some defense lawyers for witnesses advising them of forthcoming grand jury subpoenas. It was not clear how many as of Tuesday had received a subpoena or were still waiting to receive one, and the identities of the witnesses receiving subpoenas were also not immediately clear. The people who confirmed the subpoenas spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss a secretive grand jury investigation.

The Investigation Has Focused in Large Part on the Trump-Russia Probe

The contours of the conspiracy investigation aren't fully known, but agents and prosecutors over the last several months have focused intensely on one of Trump's chief grievances: the U.S. government response to Russian interference in 2016 and an intelligence community assessment that Moscow meddled on Trump's behalf at the direction of Russian President Vladimir Putin.

Trump, who spent much of his first term shadowed by an investigation into whether his campaign colluded with Russia to sway the outcome of the election, has for years lashed out at the intelligence community finding and cast it as a “deep state” conspiracy to undermine the legitimacy of his win.

Investigators searching for potential crimes in connection with the intelligence community response have conducted numerous voluntary interviews, but the subpoenas prepared for witnesses in recent days represent an apparent effort to lock down sworn testimony before a grand jury.

It remains unclear whether anyone will be charged or for what offense, though lawyers for former CIA Director John Brennan have said they have been informed that he is a target as investigators examine whether he falsely testified to Congress — something he and his attorneys have consistently denied. The Justice Department last spring subpoenaed witnesses before a Washington grand jury as part of an investigation into Brennan, but swiftly withdrew the subpoenas in favor of voluntary interviews.

The investigation is being run out of Florida, with the Justice Department in April bringing back into government service a top prosecutor from the Reagan administration, Joe diGenova, to serve as a counselor to the attorney general and help lead a team of agents and prosecutors.

diGenova, who had previously asked then-Attorney General Pam Bondi to appoint him to the job and has openly and repeatedly claimed Trump was the victim of an intelligence community conspiracy, declined to comment Tuesday when reached by The Associated Press.

In an indication of the wide-ranging nature of the investigation, the AP reported last month that diGenova's team has sought interviews with law enforcement officials involved in the 2022 FBI search of Trump’s Mar-a-Lago property in Palm Beach, Florida. The search recovered a trove of classified documents that formed the basis of a since-abandoned Justice Department prosecution of Trump, who has long decried the FBI operation as an invasion of his privacy.

Concerns From Defense Lawyers About a ‘Favored’ Judge

Investigators have set up shop in Fort Pierce, Florida, the home court of U.S. District Judge Aileen Cannon, the Trump-appointed jurist who repeatedly appeared skeptical of the classified documents case against him and ultimately dismissed it after concluding that the prosecutor who filed the charges was illegally appointed.

Lawyers for Brennan last year asked the chief judge of the federal court in Florida to prevent the investigation from being steered to Cannon, whom they described as a “favored” Trump judge. They have since sued the Trump administration, demanding a court order requiring prosecutors to preserve records from the investigation so that Brennan could challenge any eventual prosecution of him as vindictive and selective.

Trump came to office in 2017 under scrutiny from the intelligence and law enforcement community about whether his successful campaign had conspired with Russia, which stole politically damaging Democratic emails and orchestrated their release through WikiLeaks as part of a wide-ranging interference scheme.

A Justice Department special counsel, Robert Mueller, investigated but found insufficient evidence to prove a criminal conspiracy between Russia and the Trump campaign, though his team of investigators did find that Russia interfered in sweeping fashion in the election and that the campaign eagerly hoped to benefit from Moscow’s help.

Subsequent investigations by an inspector general and Justice Department prosecutors identified numerous errors and omissions by agents who conducted the Russia probe but found no evidence of criminal wrongdoing by senior law enforcement officials nor proof of an anti-Trump conspiracy like what prosecutors are now hoping to prove.

Deeply frustrated by those outcomes, Trump has amplified his demands for retribution, which his Justice Department has heeded. Last year, Bondi directed prosecutors to put evidence before a grand jury following the release of documents aimed at calling into question the legitimacy of the Trump-Russia inquiry.

entries.title: U.S. Strikes Iranian Tankers in Retaliation for Attacks on Navy Vessels
entries.summary: Iran’s Revolutionary Guard Navy has warned crews of oil tankers near ports in Kuwait and Bahrain to immediately leave their vessels.
entries.content:
By Konstantin Toropin

The U.S. has struck multiple Iranian tankers in response to more attempted missile attacks on a Navy warship, according to a U.S. official, who spoke Tuesday on condition of anonymity to discuss sensitive military operations.

It marks the latest tit-for-tat strikes as Washington and Tehran lurch back toward fighting during more than six months of war.

Iran’s Revolutionary Guard Navy has warned crews of oil tankers near ports in Kuwait and Bahrain to immediately leave their vessels, saying the ships could be targeted in retaliation for U.S. attacks on Iranian tankers.

The warning, carried by Iranian state television, said the U.S. military had targeted several Iranian oil tankers. It accused Kuwait and Bahrain of hosting U.S. forces and assisting in the attacks.

The Revolutionaly Guard warned tanker crews to abandon their vessels whether they were at anchor or docked, saying they “will be targeted.”

entries.title: 'South Park’ Creators Say the Series’ Name Is Changing Thanks to Trump
entries.summary: Showmakers Trey Parker and Matt Stone are turning the show’s 29th season debut into another mockery of the president.
entries.content:
“South Park” creators Trey Parker and Matt Stone announced that the long-running comedy show will premier its next season with a new name, one which appears to be another elaborate joke made at President Donald Trump’s expense.

“Inspired by the bravery and patriotism of Apple and Google,” Parker and Stone said in a statement Tuesday, “we are changing the name of South Park to SOUTH AMERICA.”

The mock-rebrand comes after Trump issued a series of directives and executive orders to rename geographic landmarks, notably changing Lake Ontario to Lake America and the Gulf of Mexico to Gulf of America. Apple and Google quickly complied, updating their map apps to reflect the new names.

On Labor Day morning, Trump published seven posts to his Truth Social page in a few minutes' span proposing New Mexico change its name to “New America.”

“South Park” frequently satirizes the president, notably depicting Trump in a sexual relationship with the devil. The White House returned fire last year, saying the show “hasn’t been relevant in 20 years.”

In their news release, Parker and Stone also gave “special thanks” to their parent company Paramount, which they dubbed “a Skydance Capitulation” in a nod to the company’s recent merger with Skydance, which is owned by Trump superdonor Larry Ellison.

The two often joke about their tense relationship with the company, and have openly mocked their bosses for repeatedly rolling over to political pressure by canceling “The Late Show With Stephen Colbert” and reportedly altering CBS News programming to appease the Trump administration.

“South Park” has so far survived scrutiny from Paramount, in large part due to its unusual streaming deal that keeps creative autonomy in the hands of Stone and Parker.

The 29th season of “South Park” — or “South America” — premieres Sept. 16.
