entries.title: Mega Millions-Winning Congressman Violates the STOCK Act
entries.summary: Democratic Rep. Gil Cisneros of California was late revealing more than 50 trades.
entries.content:
One of Congress’ most prolific stock traders violated a federal insider trading and transparency law by failing to properly disclose six-figures’ worth of purchases, according to new U.S. House financial records.

Rep. Gil Cisneros (D-California), who sits on the House Armed Services Committee, was days or weeks late revealing more than 50 individual trades, including shares of defense contractors Palantir Technologies, Microsoft, Macom Technology Solutions and SPX Technologies.

Other tardy disclosures by Cisneros, who won a Mega Millions jackpot worth $266 million in 2010, include trades in cryptocurrency company Coinbase Global, computer chip giant Nvidia, media conglomerate Paramount Skydance Corporation and ride-hailing platform Uber.

Taken together, Cisneros’ improperly disclosed stock trades are worth between $95,000 and $900,000. (Lawmakers are only required to list the values of their trades in broad ranges.) The records come as the U.S. Senate is considering the House-approved Stop Insider Trading Act, which would in part ban federal lawmakers from buying individual stocks.

Representatives for Cisneros acknowledged NOTUS’ request for comment but did not otherwise respond to phone and email messages.

It’s unclear whether Cisneros has or will pay a late-filing fine administered by the House Ethics Committee, which begins at $200 and may be waived at the committee’s discretion. Representatives for the committee, which is led by Rep. Michael Guest (R-Mississippi) — himself as STOCK Act violator this summer — did not respond to a request for comment.

In February, Cisneros told NOTUS that he doesn’t manage his own investments, and therefore, does not believe that his personal stock holdings conflict with his public service in Congress.

NOTUS’ Capitol Gains project estimated Cisneros’ median net worth to be $65.91 million entering 2025.

“I have a financial adviser, and you look at the size of my portfolio and you’ll understand why I have a financial adviser who makes all the decisions, and I trust him to do it,” Cisneros said. “I trust my adviser. As I always say, I got very lucky in life and I want to be able to protect it.”

Cisneros has made hundreds of other stock trades during the 119th Congress, House records indicate.

Among them: purchasing up to tens of thousands of dollars’ worth of stock in Palantir, which also has scored Immigration and Customs Enforcement contracts, and $15,000 worth of SpaceX stock days after the Elon Musk-led company made its initial public offering of stock.

In June, Cisneros easily emerged from a competitive primary to advance to November’s general election, where he’s heavily favored to win reelection to California’s 31st Congressional District, which includes parts of eastern Los Angeles County.

In addition to Guest, Cisneros joins an ever-growing list of federal lawmakers who’ve violated the STOCK Act’s disclosure provisions.

Since last summer, violators in the House include Reps. Michael Rulli (R-Ohio), Shri Thanedar (D-Michigan), Tracey Mann (R-Kansas), Julie Johnson (D-Texas), Linda Sánchez (D-California), Julia Letlow (R-Louisiana), Jim Jordan (R-Ohio), Lisa McClain (R-Michigan), Pat Ryan (D-New York), Sheri Biggs (R-South Carolina), Derek Tran (D-California), Donald Norcross (D-New Jersey), Tim Walberg (R-Michigan), Rich McCormick (R-Georgia), Ritchie Torres (D-New York), Troy Nehls (R-Texas), Dan Meuser (R-Pennsylvania), Jonathan Jackson (D-Illinois), George Whitesides (D-California), Val Hoyle (D-Oregon), Austin Scott (R-Georgia), Debbie Wasserman Schultz (D-Florida), Pramila Jayapal (D-Washington), Kelly Morrison (D-Minnesota), Christian Menefee (D-Texas), Daniel Webster (R-Florida), Ed Case (D-Hawaii), Dan Crenshaw (R-Texas), Laurel Lee (R-Florida) and Scott Franklin (R-Florida). Rep. Kevin Hern (R-Oklahoma) was also late, although his office denies it.

Senators who’ve violated the STOCK Act during the past year include Sens. Alan Armstrong (R-Oklahoma), Ron Wyden (D-Oregon), Katie Britt (R-Alabama), Susan Collins (R-Maine), John Hickenlooper (D-Colorado), Mike Rounds (R-South Dakota) and John Fetterman (D-Pennsylvania).

entries.content:
Good afternoon. This is the Final NOTUS newsletter for Sept. 8, 2026. You can get it in your inbox every day by signing up here — it’s free!

THE LATEST

Scoop: The Trump administration is planning a major shake-up at the National Park Service and will tell officials to “avoid categorical promises” about layoffs, according to internal planning documents obtained by NOTUS.

  • The nation’s 430 park units would operate dramatically differently under the proposed plan, with bigger parks given control over small ones. 
  • The Interior Department hasn’t yet notified Congress of its intention to reorganize, which it is legally obligated to do before implementation.
Smithsonian chief Lonnie Bunch III will retire at the end of this year. He told The New York Times the decision wasn’t due to pressure from the White House, but that the back-and-forth over how American history should be told did take a toll on him.

  • “I have to be honest, it has been stressful,” he told the Times. “And at a certain point, I’d like to wake up in the morning and not look at my cellphone.”




THE ADMINISTRATION

Canada’s retaliatory tariffs of up to 50% on $20 billion worth of U.S. goods went into effect Tuesday, just hours after President Donald Trump threatened to ban sales from Bombardier, a Canadian aircraft manufacturer, in the United States.

  • Bombardier’s U.S. headquarters is in Kansas, and Republicans there are not happy with the idea. 
Treasury handed out new sanctions on Iran’s already heavily targeted aviation sector, the latest in a series of measures intended to cripple the country’s economy.

Icelandic officials summoned U.S. Ambassador Billy Long after Trump posted an image to Truth Social of the arctic nation and several other countries wrapped in the American flag.

  • Minister for Foreign Affairs Þorgerður Katrín Gunnarsdóttir told Long — who had to apologize for calling Iceland the “52nd state” earlier this year — the post “was entirely unacceptable.”




THE HILL

Sen. Roger Marshall (R-Kansas), an obstetrician-gynecologist, has sued more than 700 patients for outstanding medical bills, The New York Times reports. Patients in 81 of those cases were arrested.

  • The unpaid bills ranged from $101 to several thousand dollars. Marshall’s office routinely charged an 18% annual interest rate. Payton Fuller, a spokesperson for Marshall, said on X that “Judges issue warrants, not doctors” and called the story “an obvious hit piece.” 




THE CAMPAIGN TRAIL

Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker is jumping into the midterms spending fight with a new PAC stocked with a whopping $20 million called “Ready For the Fight.”

  • The PAC’s first ad buys are against two House candidates: Rep. Max Miller in Ohio and firearms influencer Brandon Herrera in Texas.




THE WORLD

The United Kingdom, France and Canada imposed trade restrictions on Israeli settlements in the West Bank, joining a broader coalition of 12 countries that have imposed sanctions on the communities, which are illegal under international law.

  • U.S. Ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee said the move would “without a doubt” spur consequences from Washington.

entries.title: U.S. Central Command Says American Drone Captured by Iran ‘Malfunctioned’
entries.summary: Iranian state media had claimed the vehicle was one of the “most modern” and “smart” submarines.
entries.content:
U.S. Central Command said that an American submarine drone captured by Iran near the Strait of Hormuz on Tuesday “malfunctioned” and pushed back on claims by Iranian state media that it nabbed a high-tech surveillance vehicle.

A CENTCOM spokesperson, Navy Capt. Tim Hawkins, told NOTUS in a statement that the drone was surveying waters in the region to support ongoing military operations and malfunctioned more than a day ago.

“The defective drone was an older model that neither collected sensitive data nor carried any classified sonar or radar equipment,” Hawkins said. “U.S. operations in area waters continue.”

The statement counters Iranian officials who said that the underwater vehicle was one of the “most modern” and “smart” submarines and was equipped with “the latest” technology.

Iranian state-run media reported that the submarine was capable of “surveillance, seabed mapping, mine detection and inspection of submarine cables and pipelines.” Iranian state TV also released an image of the unmanned submersible vehicle on Tuesday.

The Strait of Hormuz remains locked in a military stalemate after U.S. forces struck three Iranian oil tankers following attacks on Navy warships over the weekend. The American military warned Saturday it would “if necessary, destroy Iran’s limited and exposed oil fleet.”

The incident came after President Donald Trump called the conflict “small potatoes” last week and negotiations to end the war have largely lapsed.

entries.title: DHS Asks the Supreme Court to Revive Overhauled Voter Database
entries.summary: The filing contends a lower court ruling that blocked the inclusion of some data “threatens the integrity of upcoming elections.”
entries.content:
The Trump administration asked the Supreme Court on Tuesday to allow it to use its overhauled citizenship verification system ahead of the midterm elections.

In an application, the Department of Homeland Security argues that a lower court ruling that blocked the use of Social Security numbers and other information in the Systematic Alien Verification for Entitlements, or SAVE, system, “threatens the integrity of upcoming elections.”

DHS revamped the system after President Donald Trump’s executive order in March 2025 aimed at rooting out potential noncitizen voters, although there is no evidence of large numbers of noncitizens voting in U.S. elections.

In the filing, DHS said the system has verified the citizenship of more than 65 million voters across 26 states while flagging 28,635 potential non-citizens on state voter lists. “The district court’s order, however, makes it harder to detect ineligible voters, undermining the integrity of federal elections and public confidence in the results of those elections,” the application states.

The SAVE system was created to verify the immigration status of non-citizens and naturalized U.S. citizens applying for government benefits.

Under the Trump administration, DHS has been overhauling the system to use it for voter verification, connecting additional government data to the system, including data from the Social Security Administration, and expanding its reach to also cover U.S. citizens.

That has sparked both privacy concerns and fears that the system could disenfranchise eligible voters; in Utah and Texas, some of those flagged by the system were later verified to be U.S. citizens.

States are charged with election administration under the Constitution and already have systems in place to maintain their voter rolls.

Voting and privacy groups have sued over the addition of Social Security numbers to the database — leading to the ruling from June that the Trump administration filing calls “an indefensible order that threatens the integrity of upcoming elections.”

DHS contends a district court judge got it wrong when she found the voting- and privacy-rights groups have a legal right to file the lawsuit and that the new SAVE system violates privacy law.

Last week, a federal appeals court declined to allow the federal government to revive the database.

The Trump administration says that the block on the SAVE system will “irreparably harm the federal government, the States, and the public by depriving the government of an effective tool to verify the eligibility of registered voters and benefits applicants under various state and federal programs.”

The old SAVE system, the government says, is “an older, slower, more cumbersome, and less capable process” that does not have certain identifying information and requires users to search one name at a time.

Critics, meanwhile, say that some of the data the new SAVE system relies on to verify citizens is not fit for purpose.

“Social Security numbers are not verification of citizenship,” Tina Waddell, former general counsel at SSA who left the agency last year, told NOTUS previously. The Social Security Administration itself has said that its data isn’t a definitive record of U.S. citizens.

The Trump administration’s efforts to revamp the SAVE system and use it to comb through voter rolls has been at the center of tangled legal proceedings.

The Supreme Court has ordered a response from the voting groups that challenged the database by Sept. 15..

The SAVE system is not the only front in the Trump administration’s effort to verify voter rolls and change voting in the midterms, including a challenge to a U.S. Postal Service rule over mail-in ballots.

The administration also has been attempting to obtain copies of states’ voter rolls, so far with no success.

entries.title: Challenge to Abortion Drug Heads Back to Court Ahead of Midterm Elections
entries.summary: An appeals court hears oral arguments as the Trump administration considers its broader strategy for restricting access to mifepristone.
entries.content:
A federal appeals court in Louisiana is set to hear oral arguments Wednesday in a high-profile case that could limit access to a drug used in nearly two-thirds of abortions in the United States.

The court action over whether the abortion and miscarriage drug mifepristone can continue to be distributed through the mail and telemedicine appointments, coming weeks before the midterms, is legally and politically thorny for the Trump administration.

Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. promised GOP state attorneys general a year ago that the Food and Drug Administration would review mifepristone’s safety. But the effort initially stalled amid sharp Trump administration divisions over how to handle the divisive issue in an election year.

The Justice Department is defending a Biden administration policy on mifepristone on procedural grounds at this stage, but Attorney General Todd Blanche told lawmakers during his confirmation hearing in July that the administration wants to reinstate restrictions on the drug.

Previously, patients could only get mifepristone at in-person doctor visits. The state of Louisiana, which sued the FDA last fall to reverse the Biden policy, has now asked the 5th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals to side with it on a procedural issue as the case appears destined to return to the Supreme Court.

In its initial complaint, Louisiana argued Biden-era regulators expanded access without properly considering potential safety risks. The state also claimed the policy violated the Comstock Act, which generally bars mailing of abortion drugs.

More than 20 interest groups on both sides of the abortion debate have since intervened in the case, along with the drugmakers. After ping-ponging through the court system over the past year, oral arguments will be heard by a panel of three judges — appointees of former presidents George W. Bush, Barack Obama and Joe Biden.

The case has the potential to reshape access to medication abortions, which have become the most common method for terminating a pregnancy in the four years since the Supreme Court’s conservative majority ended the constitutional right to an abortion.

“This case isn’t just about Louisiana — it could make it much harder to get abortion pills in every state, from New York to California,” said Nancy Northup, head of the Center for Reproductive Rights. “This is not simply about convenience — for many people, telehealth could be the difference between getting an abortion and not.”

Much of the case hangs on when the Trump administration will finalize its review of mifepristone. A U.S. district judge in the underlying court case challenging the policy ruled in April that Louisiana was likely to succeed on the merits but that the litigation should be paused while the FDA conducted its review.

The FDA is required to update a district court by Oct. 7 on its progress. Anti-abortion activists say they’re still not sure whether much has been done. “Hopefully it started,” said Tom McClusky, director of government affairs for CatholicVote.

One GOP Senate staffer, granted anonymity because he wasn’t authorized to speak to the press, said: “We get the clear sense that the White House doesn’t want the report to be finalized until after Election Day.”

An FDA spokesperson told NOTUS the agency is undergoing the review. “The FDA is conducting a safety study of mifepristone and is performing a review of the mifepristone REMS [Risk Evaluation and Mitigation Strategy],” the spokesperson said. “The FDA cannot comment on potential future actions or decisions.”

Acting FDA Commissioner Kyle Diamantas called anti-abortion leaders after he took the agency’s helm last spring to assure them he’d make it happen. They said they’re hopeful that Heidi Overton, President Donald Trump’s nominee for permanent commissioner, will move the study along quickly.

Activists also hope the FDA review provides the agency with justification for reinstating the in-person dispensing requirements.

And some Republican lawmakers are looking for Blanche to follow through on the legal side. Sen. Josh Hawley (R-Missouri) pressured Blanche during a confirmation hearing in July to explain why the Trump administration had left the Biden administration’s policy in place.

Hawley asked how Blanche planned to help Republican-led states out of a tangle of litigation with the Trump administration over abortion pill access. In addition to Louisiana, several other states have challenged the approval of mifepristone or the loosening of access rules.

“We are not defending what Biden did, and will not,” Blanche said, adding that the Justice Department intended to let the FDA finish its mifepristone review.

“We’re trying to let FDA — we, meaning the Department of Justice — do their work, so that we can continue to protect the lives of the unborn children and frankly the states’ laws, like Missouri’s, which is really what’s being violated here,” Blanche testified.

Blanche’s remarks line up closely with what the Justice Department’s appellate attorneys wrote in their briefs in the 5th Circuit case. Taking a technical approach to the legal issues at play, they argued that the judges should preserve the status quo and put the litigation on hold while the FDA completes its review.

Louisiana’s lawyers, however, quoted Blanche’s own words to try to persuade the judges to rule the opposite. Blanche, they wrote, was “exactly right” when he told lawmakers the policy undercut the state’s laws.

Mifepristone, developed in the 1980s, is administered in the first 10 weeks of pregnancy and works by preventing the uterus from retaining a fertilized egg. It’s one of two pills typically taken for a medication abortion.

The pills and their broad availability through the mail have kept abortion accessible to women in states with abortion bans after the Supreme Court overturned Roe v. Wade in 2022. Under 2023 Biden administration rules, women can order the pills from a doctor in another state.

Anti-abortion activists are trying to put an immediate stop to that practice, asking Blanche to settle Louisiana’s lawsuit and block the mailing of the pills.

“Mail-order mifepristone has become a public health crisis in our country,” said Kelsey Pritchard, communications director for Susan B. Anthony Pro-Life America. “This is the opportunity to end the problem.”

entries.title: The Supreme Court Leaves Missouri's 2022 Congressional Map in Place
entries.summary: At almost the same time, a federal judge in a separate lawsuit ordered state officials to keep using the newer map.
entries.content:
A legal fight over which map Missouri voters will use this November is creating its own convoluted twists and turns.

The Supreme Court on Tuesday denied a bid from Missouri to use a redrawn congressional map for the 2026 elections that targeted a Democratic-held district.

Republicans had asked the justices to step in and halt a ruling from the state’s highest court, which would have voters choose their U.S. representatives from a map used in the 2022 elections.

The decision is a win for Democrats who had fought a Republican-led redistricting that split a Kansas City seat held by Democratic Rep. Emanuel Cleaver. The old map yielded a state delegation with six Republicans and two Democrats.

Justice Brett Kavanaugh, who oversees emergency requests from the region, denied Missouri’s application without explanation.

But it may not be the final court action in the redistricting clash.

At almost the same time as the Supreme Court order, in a separate case brought by a member of Congress and others, a federal judge quickly halted the use of any map other than the one drawn this year by the Republican-controlled state legislature for two weeks while litigation plays out.

“Using a different map for the general election would wreak havoc on the fairness and orderliness of Missouri’s congressional elections, calling into question the candidacy of those nominated in the primaries and the votes of those who voted in the primaries,” Stephen R. Clark, the chief judge of the U.S. Eastern District of Missouri, said in his decision.

“Widespread voter confusion would inevitably follow,” Clark added. “The public interest factor thus weighs in favor” of a preliminary injunction.

The order will remain in effect for two weeks while Clark considers whether to extend the use of the new map through November. His order acknowledged that Kavanaugh had just denied Missouri’s application.

That decision was immediately followed by an appeal to the U.S. 8th Circuit Court from the citizens group behind the original lawsuit over the maps

The Missouri dispute is part of a nationwide wave of mid-decade redistricting ordered up by President Donald Trump to aid Republicans in protecting their narrow House majority.

Democratic-led states responded with redistricting efforts of their own.

The back-and-forth over Missouri’s electoral map comes less than two months before Election Day, amid several late-breaking court fights over election procedures, including ongoing litigation over mail-voting rules.

This story has been updated with new developments.

And some Republican lawmakers are looking for Blanche to follow through on the legal side. Sen. Josh Hawley (R-Missouri) pressured Blanche during a confirmation hearing in July to explain why the Trump administration had left the Biden administration’s policy in place.

Hawley asked how Blanche planned to help Republican-led states out of a tangle of litigation with the Trump administration over abortion pill access. In addition to Louisiana, several other states have challenged the approval of mifepristone or the loosening of access rules.

“We are not defending what Biden did, and will not,” Blanche said, adding that the Justice Department intended to let the FDA finish its mifepristone review.

“We’re trying to let FDA — we, meaning the Department of Justice — do their work, so that we can continue to protect the lives of the unborn children and frankly the states’ laws, like Missouri’s, which is really what’s being violated here,” Blanche testified.

Blanche’s remarks line up closely with what the Justice Department’s appellate attorneys wrote in their briefs in the 5th Circuit case. Taking a technical approach to the legal issues at play, they argued that the judges should preserve the status quo and put the litigation on hold while the FDA completes its review.

Louisiana’s lawyers, however, quoted Blanche’s own words to try to persuade the judges to rule the opposite. Blanche, they wrote, was “exactly right” when he told lawmakers the policy undercut the state’s laws.

Mifepristone, developed in the 1980s, is administered in the first 10 weeks of pregnancy and works by preventing the uterus from retaining a fertilized egg. It’s one of two pills typically taken for a medication abortion.

The pills and their broad availability through the mail have kept abortion accessible to women in states with abortion bans after the Supreme Court overturned Roe v. Wade in 2022. Under 2023 Biden administration rules, women can order the pills from a doctor in another state.

Anti-abortion activists are trying to put an immediate stop to that practice, asking Blanche to settle Louisiana’s lawsuit and block the mailing of the pills.

“Mail-order mifepristone has become a public health crisis in our country,” said Kelsey Pritchard, communications director for Susan B. Anthony Pro-Life America. “This is the opportunity to end the problem.”

entries.title: The Supreme Court Leaves Missouri's 2022 Congressional Map in Place
entries.summary: At almost the same time, a federal judge in a separate lawsuit ordered state officials to keep using the newer map.
entries.content:
A legal fight over which map Missouri voters will use this November is creating its own convoluted twists and turns.

The Supreme Court on Tuesday denied a bid from Missouri to use a redrawn congressional map for the 2026 elections that targeted a Democratic-held district.

Republicans had asked the justices to step in and halt a ruling from the state’s highest court, which would have voters choose their U.S. representatives from a map used in the 2022 elections.

The decision is a win for Democrats who had fought a Republican-led redistricting that split a Kansas City seat held by Democratic Rep. Emanuel Cleaver. The old map yielded a state delegation with six Republicans and two Democrats.

Justice Brett Kavanaugh, who oversees emergency requests from the region, denied Missouri’s application without explanation.

But it may not be the final court action in the redistricting clash.

At almost the same time as the Supreme Court order, in a separate case brought by a member of Congress and others, a federal judge quickly halted the use of any map other than the one drawn this year by the Republican-controlled state Legislature for two weeks while litigation plays out.

“Using a different map for the general election would wreak havoc on the fairness and orderliness of Missouri’s congressional elections, calling into question the candidacy of those nominated in the primaries and the votes of those who voted in the primaries,” Stephen R. Clark, the chief judge of the U.S. Eastern District of Missouri, said in his decision.

“Widespread voter confusion would inevitably follow,” Clark added. “The public interest factor thus weighs in favor” of a preliminary injunction.

The order will remain in effect for two weeks while Clark considers whether to extend the use of the new map through November. His order acknowledged that Kavanaugh had just denied Missouri’s application.

That decision was immediately followed by an appeal to the U.S. 8th Circuit Court from the citizens group behind the original lawsuit over the maps

The Missouri dispute is part of a nationwide wave of mid-decade redistricting ordered up by President Donald Trump to aid Republicans in protecting their narrow House majority.

Democratic-led states responded with redistricting efforts of their own.

The back-and-forth over Missouri’s electoral map comes less than two months before Election Day, amid several late-breaking court fights over election procedures, including ongoing litigation over mail-voting rules.

This story has been updated with new developments.

entries.title: Air Force Base to Allow Religious Greetings After Hegseth Vowed to Intervene
entries.summary: A spokesperson for Kirtland Air Force Base defended the use of greetings like “have a blessed day” after a religious freedom group denounced the practice.
entries.content:
Guards at a New Mexico Air Force base were cleared to continue using religious greetings while operating the facility’s gates, according to a statement provided to NOTUS — a policy that comes after complaints about the greetings spurred Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth to defend the Christian service members.

The Military Religious Freedom Foundation, a nonprofit that advocates for the separation of church and state within the military, last week reported receiving dozens of complaints regarding guards saying “Have a blessed day” or “God bless you” to people arriving at the base’s gates.

But after the headline-grabbing criticism, a spokesperson for Kirtland Air Force Base said there were no plans to police the “common phrases” that service members use to greet each other and visitors to the facility.

“Base officials have reviewed the feedback received from a small percentage of individuals with base access and, in line with Department of the Air Force policies and the law, have not issued, and have no plans to issue, any changes to procedures either mandating or restricting the use of common phrases while welcoming personnel to the installation,” base officials told NOTUS.

Kirtland base officials added that gate guards are “expected to communicate professionally and courteously” with everyone entering the facility.

Mikey Weinstein, a former Air Force captain who founded the Military Religious Freedom Foundation, told NOTUS that he did not receive a faith-based greeting when he visited the base on Monday — though he said he heard a secondhand account of the religious greetings continuing this week.

Mandatory Air Force policy requires leaders and service members to “ensure their words and actions do not discriminate against any individual or group because of their faith, belief, or absence of belief, or extend preferential treatment for the same.”

If the religious greetings continue at the base, Weinstein said his group will pursue a writ of mandamus in federal court, which is an official court order that would require the Defense Department to follow its own regulations.

Hegseth sharply criticized the Military Religious Freedom Foundation last week and promised to intervene to protect the Christian greetings.

“The MRFF is a radical anti-Christian, pro-atheist group that attacks any/all faith inside the @DeptofWar,” Hegseth wrote Friday on X. “We will never cave to them. The @usairforce will confront this.”

Air Force Chief of Staff Gen. Kenneth Wilsbach said Friday the policies on the greetings “are unchanged,” and there were no plans to restrict “the use of common greetings while entering our bases.”

The Department of Defense did not respond to a request for comment.

Weinstein called the religious greetings a “blatant violation” of Air Force regulations that threaten religious freedoms for all military members.

“When differences become divisions, you destroy the unity, morale, discipline, and good order that are the compelling governmental interests that our U.S. Supreme Court talks about when it comes to the First Amendment in the military,” Weinstein said.

entries.title: New Grand Jury Subpoenas Sent in Trump-Russia Conspiracy Probe
entries.summary: The Justice Department is demanding testimony for an investigation into the intelligence community.
entries.content:
By Eric Tucker

The Justice Department is demanding testimony before a Florida grand jury in an investigation aiming to establish an intelligence community conspiracy against President Donald Trump, according to multiple people familiar with the matter.

New subpoenas being issued to former government officials represent an escalation in the year-long investigation as the Justice Department pursues a loosely defined theory that members of the intelligence community who scrutinized Trump over the last decade, including over Russian interference in the 2016 election, conspired against him and violated his rights.

Investigators in recent days contacted some defense lawyers for witnesses advising them of forthcoming grand jury subpoenas. It was not clear how many as of Tuesday had received a subpoena or were still waiting to receive one, and the identities of the witnesses receiving subpoenas were also not immediately clear. The people who confirmed the subpoenas spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss a secretive grand jury investigation.

The Investigation Has Focused in Large Part on the Trump-Russia Probe

The contours of the conspiracy investigation aren't fully known, but agents and prosecutors over the last several months have focused intensely on one of Trump's chief grievances: the U.S. government response to Russian interference in 2016 and an intelligence community assessment that Moscow meddled on Trump's behalf at the direction of Russian President Vladimir Putin.

Trump, who spent much of his first term shadowed by an investigation into whether his campaign colluded with Russia to sway the outcome of the election, has for years lashed out at the intelligence community finding and cast it as a “deep state” conspiracy to undermine the legitimacy of his win.

Investigators searching for potential crimes in connection with the intelligence community response have conducted numerous voluntary interviews, but the subpoenas prepared for witnesses in recent days represent an apparent effort to lock down sworn testimony before a grand jury.

It remains unclear whether anyone will be charged or for what offense, though lawyers for former CIA Director John Brennan have said they have been informed that he is a target as investigators examine whether he falsely testified to Congress — something he and his attorneys have consistently denied. The Justice Department last spring subpoenaed witnesses before a Washington grand jury as part of an investigation into Brennan, but swiftly withdrew the subpoenas in favor of voluntary interviews.

The investigation is being run out of Florida, with the Justice Department in April bringing back into government service a top prosecutor from the Reagan administration, Joe diGenova, to serve as a counselor to the attorney general and help lead a team of agents and prosecutors.

diGenova, who had previously asked then-Attorney General Pam Bondi to appoint him to the job and has openly and repeatedly claimed Trump was the victim of an intelligence community conspiracy, declined to comment Tuesday when reached by The Associated Press.

In an indication of the wide-ranging nature of the investigation, the AP reported last month that diGenova's team has sought interviews with law enforcement officials involved in the 2022 FBI search of Trump’s Mar-a-Lago property in Palm Beach, Florida. The search recovered a trove of classified documents that formed the basis of a since-abandoned Justice Department prosecution of Trump, who has long decried the FBI operation as an invasion of his privacy.

Concerns From Defense Lawyers About a ‘Favored’ Judge

Investigators have set up shop in Fort Pierce, Florida, the home court of U.S. District Judge Aileen Cannon, the Trump-appointed jurist who repeatedly appeared skeptical of the classified documents case against him and ultimately dismissed it after concluding that the prosecutor who filed the charges was illegally appointed.

Lawyers for Brennan last year asked the chief judge of the federal court in Florida to prevent the investigation from being steered to Cannon, whom they described as a “favored” Trump judge. They have since sued the Trump administration, demanding a court order requiring prosecutors to preserve records from the investigation so that Brennan could challenge any eventual prosecution of him as vindictive and selective.

Trump came to office in 2017 under scrutiny from the intelligence and law enforcement community about whether his successful campaign had conspired with Russia, which stole politically damaging Democratic emails and orchestrated their release through WikiLeaks as part of a wide-ranging interference scheme.

A Justice Department special counsel, Robert Mueller, investigated but found insufficient evidence to prove a criminal conspiracy between Russia and the Trump campaign, though his team of investigators did find that Russia interfered in sweeping fashion in the election and that the campaign eagerly hoped to benefit from Moscow’s help.

Subsequent investigations by an inspector general and Justice Department prosecutors identified numerous errors and omissions by agents who conducted the Russia probe but found no evidence of criminal wrongdoing by senior law enforcement officials nor proof of an anti-Trump conspiracy like what prosecutors are now hoping to prove.

Deeply frustrated by those outcomes, Trump has amplified his demands for retribution, which his Justice Department has heeded. Last year, Bondi directed prosecutors to put evidence before a grand jury following the release of documents aimed at calling into question the legitimacy of the Trump-Russia inquiry.

entries.title: U.S. Strikes Iranian Tankers in Retaliation for Attacks on Navy Vessels
entries.summary: Iran’s Revolutionary Guard Navy has warned crews of oil tankers near ports in Kuwait and Bahrain to immediately leave their vessels.
entries.content:
By Konstantin Toropin

The U.S. has struck multiple Iranian tankers in response to more attempted missile attacks on a Navy warship, according to a U.S. official, who spoke Tuesday on condition of anonymity to discuss sensitive military operations.

It marks the latest tit-for-tat strikes as Washington and Tehran lurch back toward fighting during more than six months of war.

Iran’s Revolutionary Guard Navy has warned crews of oil tankers near ports in Kuwait and Bahrain to immediately leave their vessels, saying the ships could be targeted in retaliation for U.S. attacks on Iranian tankers.

The warning, carried by Iranian state television, said the U.S. military had targeted several Iranian oil tankers. It accused Kuwait and Bahrain of hosting U.S. forces and assisting in the attacks.

The Revolutionaly Guard warned tanker crews to abandon their vessels whether they were at anchor or docked, saying they “will be targeted.”

entries.title: 'South Park’ Creators Say the Series’ Name Is Changing Thanks to Trump
entries.summary: Showmakers Trey Parker and Matt Stone are turning the show’s 29th season debut into another mockery of the president.
entries.content:
“South Park” creators Trey Parker and Matt Stone announced that the long-running comedy show will premier its next season with a new name, one which appears to be another elaborate joke made at President Donald Trump’s expense.

“Inspired by the bravery and patriotism of Apple and Google,” Parker and Stone said in a statement Tuesday, “we are changing the name of South Park to SOUTH AMERICA.”

The mock-rebrand comes after Trump issued a series of directives and executive orders to rename geographic landmarks, notably changing Lake Ontario to Lake America and the Gulf of Mexico to Gulf of America. Apple and Google quickly complied, updating their map apps to reflect the new names.

On Labor Day morning, Trump published seven posts to his Truth Social page in a few minutes' span proposing New Mexico change its name to “New America.”

“South Park” frequently satirizes the president, notably depicting Trump in a sexual relationship with the devil. The White House returned fire last year, saying the show “hasn’t been relevant in 20 years.”

In their news release, Parker and Stone also gave “special thanks” to their parent company Paramount, which they dubbed “a Skydance Capitulation” in a nod to the company’s recent merger with Skydance, which is owned by Trump superdonor Larry Ellison.

The two often joke about their tense relationship with the company, and have openly mocked their bosses for repeatedly rolling over to political pressure by canceling “The Late Show With Stephen Colbert” and reportedly altering CBS News programming to appease the Trump administration.

“South Park” has so far survived scrutiny from Paramount, in large part due to its unusual streaming deal that keeps creative autonomy in the hands of Stone and Parker.

The 29th season of “South Park” — or “South America” — premieres Sept. 16.

entries.title: Mega Millions-Winning Congressman Violates the STOCK Act
entries.summary: Democratic Rep. Gil Cisneros of California was late revealing more than 50 trades.
entries.content:
One of Congress’ most prolific stock traders violated a federal insider trading and transparency law by failing to properly disclose six-figures’ worth of purchases, according to new U.S. House financial records.

Rep. Gil Cisneros (D-California), who sits on the House Armed Services Committee, was days or weeks late revealing more than 50 individual trades, including shares of defense contractors Palantir Technologies, Microsoft, Macom Technology Solutions and SPX Technologies.

Other tardy disclosures by Cisneros, who won a Mega Millions jackpot worth $266 million in 2010, include trades in cryptocurrency company Coinbase Global, computer chip giant Nvidia, media conglomerate Paramount Skydance Corporation and ride-hailing platform Uber.

Taken together, Cisneros’ improperly disclosed stock trades are worth between $95,000 and $900,000. (Lawmakers are only required to list the values of their trades in broad ranges.) The records come as the U.S. Senate is considering the House-approved Stop Insider Trading Act, which would in part ban federal lawmakers from buying individual stocks.

Representatives for Cisneros acknowledged NOTUS’ request for comment but did not otherwise respond to phone and email messages.

It’s unclear whether Cisneros has or will pay a late-filing fine administered by the House Ethics Committee, which begins at $200 and may be waived at the committee’s discretion. Representatives for the committee, which is led by Rep. Michael Guest (R-Mississippi) — himself as STOCK Act violator this summer — did not respond to a request for comment.

In February, Cisneros told NOTUS that he doesn’t manage his own investments, and therefore, does not believe that his personal stock holdings conflict with his public service in Congress.

NOTUS’ Capitol Gains project estimated Cisneros’ median net worth to be $65.91 million entering 2025.

“I have a financial adviser, and you look at the size of my portfolio and you’ll understand why I have a financial adviser who makes all the decisions, and I trust him to do it,” Cisneros said. “I trust my adviser. As I always say, I got very lucky in life and I want to be able to protect it.”

Cisneros has made hundreds of other stock trades during the 119th Congress, House records indicate.

Among them: purchasing up to tens of thousands of dollars’ worth of stock in Palantir, which also has scored Immigration and Customs Enforcement contracts, and $15,000 worth of SpaceX stock days after the Elon Musk-led company made its initial public offering of stock.

In June, Cisneros easily emerged from a competitive primary to advance to November’s general election, where he’s heavily favored to win reelection to California’s 31st Congressional District, which includes parts of eastern Los Angeles County.

In addition to Guest, Cisneros joins an ever-growing list of federal lawmakers who’ve violated the STOCK Act’s disclosure provisions.

Since last summer, violators in the House include Reps. Michael Rulli (R-Ohio), Shri Thanedar (D-Michigan), Tracey Mann (R-Kansas), Julie Johnson (D-Texas), Linda Sánchez (D-California), Julia Letlow (R-Louisiana), Jim Jordan (R-Ohio), Lisa McClain (R-Michigan), Pat Ryan (D-New York), Sheri Biggs (R-South Carolina), Derek Tran (D-California), Donald Norcross (D-New Jersey), Tim Walberg (R-Michigan), Rich McCormick (R-Georgia), Ritchie Torres (D-New York), Troy Nehls (R-Texas), Dan Meuser (R-Pennsylvania), Jonathan Jackson (D-Illinois), George Whitesides (D-California), Val Hoyle (D-Oregon), Austin Scott (R-Georgia), Debbie Wasserman Schultz (D-Florida), Pramila Jayapal (D-Washington), Kelly Morrison (D-Minnesota), Christian Menefee (D-Texas), Daniel Webster (R-Florida), Ed Case (D-Hawaii), Dan Crenshaw (R-Texas), Laurel Lee (R-Florida) and Scott Franklin (R-Florida). Rep. Kevin Hern (R-Oklahoma) was also late, although his office denies it.

Senators who’ve violated the STOCK Act during the past year include Sens. Alan Armstrong (R-Oklahoma), Ron Wyden (D-Oregon), Katie Britt (R-Alabama), Susan Collins (R-Maine), John Hickenlooper (D-Colorado), Mike Rounds (R-South Dakota) and John Fetterman (D-Pennsylvania).

entries.title: Scoop: Trump’s National Parks Shake-Up
entries.content:
Good afternoon. This is the Final NOTUS newsletter for Sept. 8, 2026. You can get it in your inbox every day by signing up here — it’s free!

THE LATEST

Scoop: The Trump administration is planning a major shake-up at the National Park Service and will tell officials to “avoid categorical promises” about layoffs, according to internal planning documents obtained by NOTUS.

  • The nation’s 430 park units would operate dramatically differently under the proposed plan, with bigger parks given control over small ones. 
  • The Interior Department hasn’t yet notified Congress of its intention to reorganize, which it is legally obligated to do before implementation.
Smithsonian chief Lonnie Bunch III will retire at the end of this year. He told The New York Times the decision wasn’t due to pressure from the White House, but that the back-and-forth over how American history should be told did take a toll on him.

  • “I have to be honest, it has been stressful,” he told the Times. “And at a certain point, I’d like to wake up in the morning and not look at my cellphone.”




THE ADMINISTRATION

Canada’s retaliatory tariffs of up to 50% on $20 billion worth of U.S. goods went into effect Tuesday, just hours after President Donald Trump threatened to ban sales from Bombardier, a Canadian aircraft manufacturer, in the United States.

  • Bombardier’s U.S. headquarters is in Kansas, and Republicans there are not happy with the idea. 
Treasury handed out new sanctions on Iran’s already heavily targeted aviation sector, the latest in a series of measures intended to cripple the country’s economy.

Icelandic officials summoned U.S. Ambassador Billy Long after Trump posted an image to Truth Social of the arctic nation and several other countries wrapped in the American flag.

  • Minister for Foreign Affairs Þorgerður Katrín Gunnarsdóttir told Long — who had to apologize for calling Iceland the “52nd state” earlier this year — the post “was entirely unacceptable.”




THE HILL

Sen. Roger Marshall (R-Kansas), an obstetrician-gynecologist, has sued more than 700 patients for outstanding medical bills, The New York Times reports. Patients in 81 of those cases were arrested.

  • The unpaid bills ranged from $101 to several thousand dollars. Marshall’s office routinely charged an 18% annual interest rate. Payton Fuller, a spokesperson for Marshall, said on X that “Judges issue warrants, not doctors” and called the story “an obvious hit piece.” 




THE CAMPAIGN TRAIL

Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker is jumping into the midterms spending fight with a new PAC stocked with a whopping $20 million called “Ready For the Fight.”

  • The PAC’s first ad buys are against two House candidates: Rep. Max Miller in Ohio and firearms influencer Brandon Herrera in Texas.




THE WORLD

The United Kingdom, France and Canada imposed trade restrictions on Israeli settlements in the West Bank, joining a broader coalition of 12 countries that have imposed sanctions on the communities, which are illegal under international law.

  • U.S. Ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee said the move would “without a doubt” spur consequences from Washington.

entries.title: U.S. Central Command Says American Drone Captured by Iran ‘Malfunctioned’
entries.summary: Iranian state media had claimed the vehicle was one of the “most modern” and “smart” submarines.
entries.content:
U.S. Central Command said that an American submarine drone captured by Iran near the Strait of Hormuz on Tuesday “malfunctioned” and pushed back on claims by Iranian state media that it nabbed a high-tech surveillance vehicle.

A CENTCOM spokesperson, Navy Capt. Tim Hawkins, told NOTUS in a statement that the drone was surveying waters in the region to support ongoing military operations and malfunctioned more than a day ago.

“The defective drone was an older model that neither collected sensitive data nor carried any classified sonar or radar equipment,” Hawkins said. “U.S. operations in area waters continue.”

The statement counters Iranian officials who said that the underwater vehicle was one of the “most modern” and “smart” submarines and was equipped with “the latest” technology.

Iranian state-run media reported that the submarine was capable of “surveillance, seabed mapping, mine detection and inspection of submarine cables and pipelines.” Iranian state TV also released an image of the unmanned submersible vehicle on Tuesday.

A spokesperson for Anduril, which manufactures the vehicle, issued a statement later Tuesday.

“Dive-LD is an attritable autonomous system, meaning it is designed from the outset to operate in dangerous environments where loss of the vehicle is an expected possibility,” the spokesperson said. “Its purpose is to keep warfighters out of the most dangerous parts of the undersea mission. This vehicle had already delivered significant value operating thousands of hours in months-long operations in CENTCOM.”

The Strait of Hormuz remains locked in a military stalemate after U.S. forces struck three Iranian oil tankers following attacks on Navy warships over the weekend. The American military warned Saturday it would “if necessary, destroy Iran’s limited and exposed oil fleet.”

The incident came after President Donald Trump called the conflict “small potatoes” last week and negotiations to end the war have largely lapsed.

This story has been updated to include a statement from Anduril.

entries.title: DHS Asks the Supreme Court to Revive Overhauled Voter Database
entries.summary: The filing contends a lower court ruling that blocked the inclusion of some data “threatens the integrity of upcoming elections.”
entries.content:
The Trump administration asked the Supreme Court on Tuesday to allow it to use its overhauled citizenship verification system ahead of the midterm elections.

In an application, the Department of Homeland Security argues that a lower court ruling that blocked the use of Social Security numbers and other information in the Systematic Alien Verification for Entitlements, or SAVE, system, “threatens the integrity of upcoming elections.”

DHS revamped the system after President Donald Trump’s executive order in March 2025 aimed at rooting out potential noncitizen voters, although there is no evidence of large numbers of noncitizens voting in U.S. elections.

In the filing, DHS said the system has verified the citizenship of more than 65 million voters across 26 states while flagging 28,635 potential non-citizens on state voter lists. “The district court’s order, however, makes it harder to detect ineligible voters, undermining the integrity of federal elections and public confidence in the results of those elections,” the application states.

The SAVE system was created to verify the immigration status of non-citizens and naturalized U.S. citizens applying for government benefits.

Under the Trump administration, DHS has been overhauling the system to use it for voter verification, connecting additional government data to the system, including data from the Social Security Administration, and expanding its reach to also cover U.S. citizens.

That has sparked both privacy concerns and fears that the system could disenfranchise eligible voters; in Utah and Texas, some of those flagged by the system were later verified to be U.S. citizens.

States are charged with election administration under the Constitution and already have systems in place to maintain their voter rolls.

Voting and privacy groups have sued over the addition of Social Security numbers to the database — leading to the ruling from June that the Trump administration filing calls “an indefensible order that threatens the integrity of upcoming elections.”

DHS contends a district court judge got it wrong when she found the voting- and privacy-rights groups have a legal right to file the lawsuit and that the new SAVE system violates privacy law.

Last week, a federal appeals court declined to allow the federal government to revive the database.

The Trump administration says that the block on the SAVE system will “irreparably harm the federal government, the States, and the public by depriving the government of an effective tool to verify the eligibility of registered voters and benefits applicants under various state and federal programs.”

The old SAVE system, the government says, is “an older, slower, more cumbersome, and less capable process” that does not have certain identifying information and requires users to search one name at a time.

Critics, meanwhile, say that some of the data the new SAVE system relies on to verify citizens is not fit for purpose.

“Social Security numbers are not verification of citizenship,” Tina Waddell, former general counsel at SSA who left the agency last year, told NOTUS previously. The Social Security Administration itself has said that its data isn’t a definitive record of U.S. citizens.

The Trump administration’s efforts to revamp the SAVE system and use it to comb through voter rolls has been at the center of tangled legal proceedings.

The Supreme Court has ordered a response from the voting groups that challenged the database by Sept. 15..

The SAVE system is not the only front in the Trump administration’s effort to verify voter rolls and change voting in the midterms, including a challenge to a U.S. Postal Service rule over mail-in ballots.

The administration also has been attempting to obtain copies of states’ voter rolls, so far with no success.

entries.title: Iceland Summons U.S. Ambassador for a Rebuke Over Trump’s Truth Social Post
entries.summary: Billy Long had been forced to apologize for an earlier joke he made calling Iceland the “52nd state.”
entries.content:
The U.S. ambassador to Iceland, Billy Long, was summoned by the country’s officials for a meeting on Monday just hours after President Donald Trump posted an image to Truth Social of the Arctic nation blanketed in the American flag.

Trump posted a stylized map of North and Central American nations — including Canada, the U.S., Mexico, Greenland and Iceland — covered in the stars and stripes during a posting spree to Truth Social on Sunday, an apparent indication of his interest in taking control of those countries. Trump also shared a bizarre series of AI-generated images of “Iran's Navy” on the ocean floor, the moon and the Strait of Hormuz as American territories and New Mexico renamed “New America.”

The posts caught the attention of Icelandic officials, who have tangled with the Trump administration since the president returned to office last year.

"It was made clear to him in the meeting that the post was entirely unacceptable," Iceland's Minister for Foreign Affairs Þorgerður Katrín Gunnarsdóttir told broadcaster RÚV of her meeting with Long.

“If this is supposed to be a joke, then it is a bad joke,” she added at a press conference Tuesday, according to Arctic Today.

This isn’t the first time that Long has faced scrutiny over U.S. annexation threats. Long apologized before the Senate Foreign Relations Committee in February over a joke he made, first reported by Politico, to former House colleagues calling Iceland the “52nd state” and saying he’d serve as its governor.

“It was totally inappropriate,” Long told senators at the time. “I just hope that the people in Iceland will give me a second chance to make a first impression.”

Icelanders launched a petition earlier this year calling for Gunnarsdóttir to oust Long, with the effort garnering nearly 5,500 signatures.

Long joins a group of other Trump-tapped ambassadors who have faced removal campaigns and diplomatic rebukes.

Pete Hoekstra, the U.S. ambassador to Canada, currently faces a removal petition that has accumulated nearly 270,000 signatures — an outgrowth of the escalating U.S.-Canada trade war.

Bill White, the U.S. ambassador to Belgium, has been summoned by the country’s officials twice this year — most recently to answer for an incendiary social media post in which he mocked the country’s health minister.

Trump’s post of an American flag-covered map has renewed fears in the region of a potential U.S. annexation of Iceland's close neighbor, Greenland.

Shortly after the start of his second term, Trump pushed for the U.S. to take control of Greenland. Last January, the president even said that conversations with NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte at the World Economic Forum in Davos, Switzerland, had generated “the framework of a future deal” on Greenland.

Trump maintains that Greenland, which is a Danish territory, is vital for U.S. national security, but the push has landed with a thud in Europe — particularly in Denmark, which launched massive protests in response to the president’s push for control in the Arctic.

Iceland also joined Denmark, Finland, Iceland, Norway and Sweden in a joint statement in January defending Greenland from Trump's annexation threats.

“We collectively reiterate that matters concerning Denmark and Greenland are for Denmark and Greenland to decide alone,” the foreign ministers of each country wrote.

entries.title: Trump Administration Removes Criticism of Confederate Memorial From Arlington Cemetery
entries.summary: A marker at the memorial’s former site no longer says it provided a “mythologized” vision of the Confederacy.
entries.content:
The Trump administration censored language criticizing a monument to the Confederacy that previously stood at Arlington National Cemetery, removing a reference to the memorial’s “nostalgic, mythologized vision.”

The bronze statue depicting Confederate soldiers alongside enslaved people stood for more than a century before being removed in 2023 as part of a congressional mandate to remove symbols honoring the Confederacy on U.S. military property. The cemetery’s website described the memorial as showing “a nostalgic, mythologized vision of the Confederacy, including highly sanitized depictions of slavery.”

That language, along with further explanation of how history has “denied the horrors of slavery,” has been scrubbed ahead of a planned reinstallment next year. A marker at the former memorial site has also been replaced, with the new version missing any mention of slavery.

“Our website serves to provide facts for all visitors regarding monuments and memorials. Arlington National Cemetery’s decision to update  website language and signage at Section 16 was made to ensure it was succinct, factual, current and objective,” a cemetery spokesperson said. 

Historian Karen Cox said the language removed from the website was “absolutely accurate” historical context around the statue, which plays into the false idea that the South didn’t fight the Civil War to keep slavery but rather to protect states’ rights.

“Built into that narrative are lies,” she said. “It’s an attempt by the South to justify the confederacy, justify its role in the war and provide this gauzy haze over the Old South and slavery.”

Cox said the statue has been drawn into the GOP culture war as the Trump administration pushes back on what it calls “woke history” and attacks the discipline as a whole.

Last year, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said in a social media post announcing the return of the statue that it should never have been taken down. He referred to it as “The Reconciliation Monument.”

“Unlike the Left, we don’t believe in erasing American history — we honor it,” he wrote.

President Donald Trump has ordered the revision of multiple exhibits and descriptions of slavery and racism since his return to the White House as part of an effort to remove references to “corrosive ideology.” From Boston’s Bunker Hill to Washington’s Smithsonian institutions, discussions of race have been altered, removed or censored.

The debate over Confederate statues heated up in 2015 after a shooting killed nine congregation members at Emanuel African Methodist Episcopal Church, a historically Black church in Charleston, South Carolina. After protests across the U.S., some cities began removing statues that honored Confederate soldiers and generals. Almost 150 statues were removed between 2015 and 2020.

Trump has worked to replace some of them, including a sculpture of Confederate Gen. Albert Pike that stood in D.C.’s Judiciary Square until 2020 when protestors tore it down and set it on fire. The statue was re-erected last year, and is the only outdoor monument in D.C. to honor a Confederate general.

This story was updated with a comment from an Arlington National Cemetery spokesperson.

entries.title: Smithsonian Head Announces His Retirement After Months of Criticism From Trump
entries.summary: Lonnie Bunch III will retire at the end of 2026, wrapping up a nearly eight-year tenure as the institution’s leader.
entries.content:
Smithsonian Secretary Lonnie Bunch III announced Tuesday that he will retire at the end of the year, wrapping up a nearly eight-year tenure as the institution’s leader.

His departure comes as the Smithsonian faces mounting pressure from the Trump administration over how it tells American history. In an interview with The New York Times, Bunch said it was not the pressure from the White House that led to his departure, but that the back-and-forth did take a toll on him.

“I have to be honest, it has been stressful,” Bunch, who in 2019 became the 14th secretary of the Smithsonian and its first Black leader, told the Times. “And at a certain point, I’d like to wake up in the morning and not look at my cellphone.”

Sign up for the NOTUS Metro newsletter for essential coverage of the D.C. region.

His departure comes at a consequential moment for the Smithsonian. The Trump administration has spent more than a year criticizing the institutions’ exhibits and scholarship — pushing for a more patriotic telling of American history that focuses less on divisive issues.

Bunch has resisted that pressure, while arguing that the Smithsonian’s job is to present history in all its complexity.

“Every day, I have somebody talk to me about how important it is to have complexity and nuance,” Bunch said earlier this year. He said visitors often come away from Smithsonian exhibitions understanding something they had not known before.

Chief Justice John Roberts, the chancellor of the Smithsonian, said in a statement that Bunch had “pursued excellence in the telling of our nation’s story.”

But President Donald Trump and his top officials have struck a different tune. In March, the president released an executive order critiquing the National Museum of African American History and Culture and the Smithsonian American Women’s History Museum, among other institutions, for “a concerted and widespread effort to rewrite our Nation’s history.” 

Last month, Trump also issued another order titled “Restoring Trust in the Smithsonian,” in which he says leadership of the institution “cannot be trusted to tell America’s story with honesty and gratitude.” 

The executive order came after a White House report on the Smithsonian’s National Museum of American History that argued the museum has shifted from presenting a balanced, patriotic account of U.S. history toward what the authors characterize as progressive political activism. 

As evidence, they cited curators’ emphasis on racism, oppression and inequality while minimizing America’s founders and their achievements. The report called for the museum to return to a more “unifying” presentation of American history.

Bunch pushed back against the report, sending out a memo to Smithsonian staff in which he said that the report was not a fair representation of the museum's work and the complexity of American history. 

“While there will always be room for improvement, this report is not a fair characterization of the work and totality of the National Museum of American History," Bunch said in the memo. “We remain focused on what grounds us: a steadfast commitment to scholarship, nonpartisanship, independence, accuracy, and integrity.”

Bunch was nominated to the storied institution’s top job after spending years with the organization, most notably as the founding director of the National Museum of African American History and Culture, overseeing the creation and opening of a new museum on the National Mall in 2016.

Bunch began his Smithsonian career in 1978 as an education specialist at the National Air and Space Museum. Then, in 1983, he became the curator of history and program manager at the California Afro-American Museum. He was recruited to rejoin the Smithsonian in 1989 as supervisory curator at the National Museum of American History.

Over his career, he focused primarily on how museums can tell a more complete American story by confronting both the country’s achievements and its failures.

entries.title: Pritzker Jumps Into Midterms Money Battle With New $20M PAC
entries.summary: Pritzker, a potential 2028 Democratic presidential contender, plans to target Ohio’s Rep. Max Miller and Texas’ Brandon Herrera with ad buys.
entries.content:
Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker launched a new political action committee over the weekend that plans to funnel millions of dollars into Democratic House races ahead of the midterms.

Pritzker’s Ready for the Fight PAC — a phrase often used by the governor and repeated liberally in the committee’s first ad spot — plans to invest at least $20 million in what it considers to be overlooked and competitive races, according to Politico, which reported first on the spending push.

The committee will soon target what it deems “the worst of the worst MAGA Republicans,” with ad reservations against Rep. Max Miller (R-Ohio), who’s facing allegations of domestic abuse, and Texas’ Brandon Herrera, an incendiary internet personality who specializes in firearms and calls himself the “AK Guy.”

Both Ohio’s 7th Congressional District and Texas’ 23rd Congressional District lean red, but Pritzker sees them as potential wins for Democrats — with Trump’s approval rating dropping to record lows and midterm elections historically fairing well for the party that doesn't control the White House.

“As the affordability crisis continues, Democrats must think big and take the fight to every corner to support candidates in often-overlooked races,” a press release on the PAC reads. “With everything we care about on the line, Democrats cannot retreat to a handful of battleground races.”

The governor is seen as a potential 2028 presidential contender for Democrats and often stands in strong opposition to President Donald Trump and his policies.

This week, Pritzker will be in Dallas with other Democrats to counter the inaugural GOP midterm convention, according to CNN.

In August 2025, Pritzker hosted a group of Texas lawmakers who fled the state to oppose a Trump-backed redistricting effort. Pritzker has also fought back against Trump’s tariffs that affect the Illinois soybean industry and has lambasted the president’s immigration policies.

Pritzker is running for his third term as Illinois governor, and this PAC will bring his fight against Trump’s agenda to the national stage ahead of the midterms — and a potential presidential run.

“Since launching his campaign in 2017, Gov. Pritzker has closed his speeches with the same question: are you ready for the fight? As Gov. Pritzker has proven in Illinois, Democrats can aggressively fight Trump’s dangerous agenda and deliver real results for working families,” the press release reads.

entries.title: U.S. Hits Iran's Aviation Industry With Crippling Sanctions
entries.summary: The Trump administration accused the 36 entities targeted this week of supporting the Islamic Republic's efforts to use its aviation sector to move weapons, personnel, and illicit cargo.
entries.content:
By Farnoush Amiri

The Trump administration on Tuesday imposed sanctions on additional elements of Iran's aviation industry, targeting more than two dozen commercial and private airlines as well as foreign cargo service providers in its new push to isolate Tehran from its remaining trading partners.

The latest actions are part of the Trump administration’s Operation Economic Outcast campaign that is aimed at severing “critical financial lifelines” for the already heavily sanctioned Iranian government. The new penalties target the remaining facets of Tehran’s already beleaguered aviation ecosystem, which Washington has sanctioned for years.

“Let this be a warning to anyone doing business with Iran’s remaining airlines, all of which we sanctioned today: You are at risk of being cut off from the global financial system,” Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said in a press release.

The Trump administration accused the 36 entities targeted this week of supporting the Islamic Republic's efforts to use its aviation sector to move weapons, personnel, and illicit cargo. The moves will subject foreign firms and governments that do business with the targeted entities to sanctions themselves, including a freeze on any assets they may have in U.S. jurisdictions.

In a post on X, Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi called out the longstanding U.S. sanctions campaign against Iran, saying that the fallout “has been disastrous for America, including its standing worldwide.”

“After failing to achieve its aims through sanctions or war, Washington’s “novel” solution is…more sanctions. Seriously?” Araghchi wrote Tuesday afternoon.

The administration also claimed that private entities based in Turkey, the United Arab Emirates, Kazakhstan and Malaysia have provided parts and logistics services to Iran’s Mahan Air. The major airline, which flies from Tehran to a few dozen destinations in Asia, Europe and the Middle East, has been subject to U.S. counterterrorism sanctions since 2019 for its support for Iran’s paramilitary Revolutionary Guard, which the State Department has designated a foreign terrorist organization.

The airline was first targeted by the U.S. under the Obama administration in 2011, when it accused Mahan Air of being used to send weapons to Iranian proxies in Lebanon and Yemen.

The latest sanctions campaign is part of a two-pronged economic and military approach by President Donald Trump as he struggles to bring an end to a more than six-month-old war with Tehran.

Last week, the U.S. announced penalties against Golden Global Yatirim Bankasi Anonim Sirketi, a Turkish bank, which it accused of being established to enable Iran’s efforts to transfer oil revenues from China to Turkey, where they could then be converted to cash and gold.

The U.S. also said the institution “knowingly offered” banking services to Iranian financial entities, including those already sanctioned by the U.S. government in 2022 for funneling Tehran’s oil sales.

An Egyptian bank’s operations in the United Arab Emirates were also limited last month as part of the campaign, but the administration stopped short of imposing sanctions as it grapples with how to sever Iran's economic footprint without upending the global financial system.

entries.title: Canada Seeks Closer Ties to Europe as It Hits the U.S. With Billions in Tariffs
entries.summary: Canada is exploring ties with the European Union that could stop just short of membership, a Canadian official familiar with the discussions said.
entries.content:
By Rob Gillies

TORONTO (AP) — Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney said Tuesday that Canada would move faster to reduce its economic reliance on the United States and deepen ties with Europe as retaliatory tariffs took effect on about $20 billion worth of U.S. goods and the country braced for U.S. President Donald Trump’s response.

“In too many areas, they wanted dependency, not a true economic partnership,” Carney said in a prerecorded video outlining his government’s plan to withstand the trade war. The prime minister said four decades of deeper economic integration had left Canada too reliant on the U.S.

Canada is exploring ties with the European Union that could stop just short of membership, a Canadian official familiar with the discussions said.

Options could include expanding existing agreements, negotiating a new treaty or creating other forms of cooperation. The official said Canada is already consulting provinces, territories and labor groups about what a deeper relationship with the EU could look like, but no model has been chosen.

The official spoke on condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to discuss the talks publicly.

Carney is due in Strasbourg, France, next week, where he will attend European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen’s State of the European Union address Sept. 16 and address the European Parliament the following day.

The trade war began after Trump returned to office and imposed a series of tariffs on Canadian goods despite having negotiated and repeatedly praised the North American trade agreement during his first term. Many of those tariffs violate the pact.

The rupture is especially striking because the countries have long shared one of the world’s closest relationships, with deeply integrated economies, close defense and security cooperation, vast cultural ties and, before relations deteriorated, about 400,000 people crossing the border each day.

Canada looks beyond the US

The latest U.S. trade actions will cause short-term pain, Carney acknowledged, but he said they would push Canada to move faster on investment, infrastructure and trade diversification. He acknowledged the shift would be costly but said standing still would cost more.

Carney contrasted Canada’s deteriorating relationship with Washington with its push to deepen ties elsewhere. “For the past year and a half, we have been steering our economy toward trusted partners,” he said.

“It was easy business, but it meant we relied too much on one economic partner,” he said. “That time is over.”

Canada retaliates as Trump response looms

Carney defended the retaliation, saying Canada was matching the latest U.S. measures dollar for dollar while supporting affected workers and industries and accelerating efforts to expand trade with other countries.

“We can’t let American goods into Canada tariff-free while they charge our companies to export to them,” he said.

Canada was not seeking to escalate the confrontation, he said, but the tariffs were necessary to protect Canadian workers.

The prime minister also defended Canada’s decision to walk away from the talks, saying Washington sought limits on French-language and cultural protections, influence over future trade deals, and terms that would weaken the auto, steel and forestry sectors.

How the trade war ends could carry consequences far beyond Canada, testing whether a smaller U.S. ally can resist Trump’s economic pressure without being forced to yield.

U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer has suggested Washington could retaliate by blocking some Canadian products from the U.S. market.

The Canadian official said Ottawa does not intend to change course regardless of whether Trump responds with nothing or what the official called a “nuclear response.” The government’s strategy will remain focused on building more at home and diversifying trade abroad, the official said.

The tariffs hit hundreds of American products, including steel, aluminum, cheese, appliances, clothing, cosmetics and farm equipment, at rates of 15%, 25% or 50%. They cover about $20 billion in American goods, roughly 6% of the $333.6 billion the United States exported to Canada last year.

Since Canada-U.S. trade talks collapsed Aug. 21, Trump and his administration have imposed additional tariffs and issued a series of threats and attacks portraying Canada as weak and dependent.

Trump’s trade war and repeated talk of making Canada the 51st state have fueled anger and rallied support for Carney. Canadians have sharply cut travel to the United States and boycotted U.S. goods.

Carney praised those efforts, saying “every time we choose to buy Canadian and travel in Canada, we are sending a message that nobody is in the stands, 40 million of us are on the ice.”

Neither side is rushing back to the table

Gabriel Brunet, a spokesman for Canada-U.S. Trade Minister Dominic LeBlanc, said officials from both countries remain in contact even though formal negotiations have not resumed.

“Canadian and American officials have maintained ongoing discussions on a range of issues, although formal trade negotiations are not taking place at this stage,” Brunet said.

Former U.S. trade official Wendy Cutler said neither side appeared eager to make the first move.

“With a growing public approval rating now topping 70%, Prime Minister Carney is not in any hurry to reach out to Washington. But importantly, he has not closed the door to talks,” she said. “Clearly, at this point each side does not want to look too anxious to reengage in fear of looking weak.”

Associated Press writer Paul Wiseman in Washington contributed to this report.
